News.title: Online racism against England stars 'doubled on World Cup match days and skyrocketed after Argentina loss'
News.content:
Online racism against England stars 'doubled on World Cup match days and skyrocketed after Argentina loss'

Racist abuse against England’s football stars during the World Cup doubled on match days and skyrocketed by 10 times after the team was knocked out by Argentina, grim research shows

View 3 Images HOPE not hate found more than 5,500 explicitly racist posts directed at the England squad on X during the tournament (Image: Martin Rickett/PA Wire)

Racist abuse against England’s football stars during the World Cup doubled on match days and skyrocketed by 10 times after the team was knocked out by Argentina, grim research shows.

‌



HOPE not hate (HNH) found more than 5,500 explicitly racist posts directed at the England squad, after tracking around 320,000 posts on X, formerly Twitter, during the tournament.

‌



Researchers said baseline racial abuse accounted for 1-2% of posts throughout the tournament and more than doubled to 4-5% on match days. It rose by 10 times the normal level following England’s semi-final exit against Argentina.

‌



The study found Jude Bellingham faced the highest overall volume of racist posts. Kobbie Mainoo and Bukayo Saka suffered the highest proportion of racist abuse relative to total mentions about them, it found.

View 3 Images The study found Jude Bellingham faced the highest overall volume of racist posts (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

Djed Spence was targeted with distinct waves of anti-Muslim hate following his conversion to Islam, HNH said. The 26-year-old Inter Milan player became the first Muslim to play for the senior England men's football team when he came on as a substitute during a World Cup qualifier in September.

‌



Around one third of racist posts were sent directly to players or the England team account. Most of the abuse was posted elsewhere and referred to the team and players in the third person.

HNH said its research demonstrates how single posts by high-profile figures become “hate hubs where thousands of abusive comments gather”.

For example, it highlighted a post by Restore leader Rupert Lowe that simply said “Jude Bellingham” after the hero player scored during stoppage time at the end of the first half against Norway in the quarter-finals.

‌



HNH said the post, which received more than 13 million views, saw a barrage of racist responses, including one saying: “Deport after half-time.” Another reply said: “England 'celebrates' diversity. Remigration is the moderate approach.”

Remigration is a far-right concept referring to the deportation or voluntary return of non-white people to their so-called origin or home country.

View 3 Images Experts have long accused X, which is owned by tech billionaire Elon Musk, of amplifying harmful and extremist content using its powerful algorithms (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



HNH's research looked at posts mentioning the England team alongside terms concerning Englishness, deportation, remigration, ancestry, racial slurs, or animalisation.

Experts have long accused X, which is owned by tech billionaire Elon Musk, of amplifying harmful and extremist content using its powerful algorithms.

Patrik Hermansson, senior researcher at HOPE not hate, said there is a well-known pattern of abuse surrounding major football tournaments. England players Jadon Sancho, Marcus Rashford and Bukayo Saka faced a barrage of racism after missing penalties during the Euro 2020 final shootout, where the Three Lions lost against Italy.

‌



Jonathan Best, a football fan who livestreamed himself on Facebook racially abusing the players, was jailed in 2021. In 2022, Hugh Laidlaw was fined and given a suspended sentence after sending "hateful and racist" posts.

HNH is calling for algorithms that fuel abuse to be outlawed. It wants media regulator Ofcom to enforce safety-by-design requirements for platforms, rather than using the Online Safety Act (OSA) to address harm after it has already happened.

HNH is also calling on Ofcom to extend its crisis protocols to cover major sporting events. The protocols were developed amid recent instances of online hate having been blamed for violent riots on Britain's streets.

‌



Ofcom should also update its regulatory Codes under the OSA to designate major sporting tournaments as high-risk public events, the campaign group added.

Mr Hermansson said: “Our research shows that hate targeting footballers follows a clear and predictable pattern. It focuses on specific players and is, to a significant degree, driven by a small number of high-profile actors who benefit from the anger and attention they generate.

"What is especially troubling is that we have seen the same pattern at previous tournaments, yet very little has been done to address it. This is not new or unexpected, and platforms should no longer be able to treat it as such.”

‌



Taylor Gese, from the Future of Tech Institute, said: “The tech platforms already have the tools to stop this abuse, and Ofcom already has the mandate to enforce it - yet neither is acting. Platforms refuse to deploy their own safety controls because outrage drives engagement, and hate sells.

"Meanwhile, our regulators are turning a blind eye and letting them off the hook. It is high time Ofcom used its powers under the OSA to outlaw the toxic algorithms that harm our athletes, our children, our democracy and more.”

An Ofcom spokesman said: “No-one should have to put up with this vile abuse, and we condemn racism in all its forms. Tech firms have a legal responsibility to assess and mitigate the risk of UK users encountering criminal content, and we’ve shown we’ll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short.

Article continues below

“We have a live compliance programme open to assess whether the largest social media sites have adequate systems and processes for dealing with illegal hate speech that has been reported to them, and we’re working closely with police and footballing bodies as part of this."

News.title: 'Shoreham tragedy must force action on water safety — as no parent should have to learn the hard way'
News.content:
'Shoreham tragedy must force action on water safety — as no parent should have to learn the hard way'

Hassan El-Khawas, 55, his partner Zeina Alayn, 37, and their 14-year-old daughter Sara El-Khawas are thought to have gone into the water to swim near Shoreham Fort in Shoreham-by-Sea

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

The deaths of Hossam Al-Khawas, his wife Zeina Alayn and their 14-year-old daughter Sara are almost impossible to comprehend. A family day by the water ended with three lives lost and a six-year-old girl critically ill in hospital.

‌



There will be time to establish exactly what happened at Shoreham Harbour and whether the steep seabed or other dangers played a part.

‌



But once again, Britain has been confronted by the terrifying speed with which a day by the water can turn into tragedy. That is why the Mirror’s Save Lives for Sam campaign is so important. We are fighting for better water safety education, clearer warnings and stronger protection at places where families swim, paddle and play. Hidden dangers must be identified before more people pay such an unbearable price.

‌



No parent should discover the risks only when it is already too late. The grief facing this family is unimaginable. We owe it to them, and to every child near water, to make safety impossible to ignore.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle plan move back to UK in matter of weeks READ MORE :

Show racism the red card

England’s footballers should be remembered for what they did on the pitch, not subjected to vile racist abuse because of the colour of their skin or their faith. Yet research showing attacks doubled on match days and surged tenfold after defeat to Argentina exposes an ugly sickness that still festers around our national game.

Article continues below

Jude Bellingham, Kobbie Mainoo, Bukayo Saka and Djed Spence are young men representing their country at the highest level. They deserve pride and support, not hatred from cowards hiding behind social media accounts. Football authorities, social media companies and the police must treat this abuse with the seriousness it deserves. We have heard enough promises about stamping racism out of football.

AI can't even talk the talk

Artificial intelligence may be able to write essays, diagnose problems and conquer the digital world, but apparently a broad Yorkshire accent remains beyond its reach. Rotherham patients are struggling to make AI receptionist EMMA understand them. Perhaps the machines are not quite ready to take over after all.

News.title: Parents warned vapes are not a 'harmless part of growing up' - and instead can cause serious health issues
News.content:
Parents warned vapes are not a 'harmless part of growing up' - and instead can cause serious health issues

The new review, published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood, saw experts from the college review all published studies involving health or social outcomes of vaping on children and young people

View 3 Images A school boy vapes near his home (file image) (Image: SWNS)

Parents are being warned by leading children's doctors that vaping "should not be seen as a harmless part of growing up".

‌



A huge review says a "concerning picture is emerging" showing vapes are linked to higher rates of breathing problems in children and young people. Young people who vape are more likely to report coughs, wheezing, bronchitis symptoms and asthma flare ups.

‌



Their vape use is also linked to allergies, sleep issues, eye symptoms and damage to oral and dental health including inflammation and ulcers. It also has links to mental health problems including anxiety, depression and panic disorder.

‌



Vapes can help stop people stop smoking and are considered a less risky choice than cigarettes. But they are often packaged colourfully to target children and have massive choice of flavours including candy and bubblegum.

Woman's harrowing last four words as she dies of lung problems after vaping habit READ MORE :

View 3 Images One in ten school children currently vape (Image: Getty Images)

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) - who carried out the ‘most comprehensive reviews to date’ - warn that long-term studies show young people who vape are significantly more likely to go on to smoke cigarettes. They are calling on the Government to put in place new rules to cut the number of flavours available and make them less tempting to children.

‌



Nearly one in ten secondary school pupils currently vape according to the Children’s Society and one in four 11 to 15 year old have tried vaping. The RCPCH said there is also evidence of harm in babies whose mothers vaped while pregnant, including abnormal reflexes, lower motor maturity, poorer self-regulation and higher risks of low weight gain.

The new review, published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood, examined more than 14,000 published articles and looked at evidence from 81 studies.

The Government in June launched a crackdown on vapes targeting kids with a shift to plain white packaging. There will also be restrictions on flavour names - to simple recognisable descriptions - and vape devices - to be white, black or grey.

‌



Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, James Murray, said: The evidence is clear: there are too many young people experimenting with vapes, attracted by the array of flavours, bright colours and marketing displays.

"We want a healthier future for the next generation, so we must act now to reduce the appeal of addictive vapes to our children."

New UK vaping laws, including a complete ban on single-use disposable vapes, first came into force in June 2025. But from October 29th this year, the age of sale for all vaping and nicotine products will be aged 18 and over. It will be an offence to sell these products to a person under the age of 18. Fines could be up to £2,500.

‌



It will also be an offence for anyone aged 18 or over to buy, or attempt to buy, vaping or nicotine products on behalf of a person under the age of 18. Government rules also require vape shops to obscure windows so products cannot be seen within 9.8ft (3m) of the door in a move designed to protect children "from exposure to the advertising of vaping".

View 3 Images The Government plan to get rid of colourful packaging for vapes (Image: Getty Images)

Co-author of the systematic review, Professor Will Carroll, welcomed these measures but said the Government “must go further.”

‌



“Vaping should not be seen as a harmless part of growing up. The evidence shows clear links with respiratory symptoms, nicotine dependence and subsequent cigarette smoking, while concerns about wider impacts on young people’s health continue to grow.

“...Current proposals will place restrictions on vape flavour names and packaging descriptions, moving away from enticing names inspired by sweets, desserts, and alcohol in favour of simple, factual names like 'apple'.

“As paediatricians, we call on the Government to limit the types of flavours available, as opposed to just their descriptions.”

‌



RCPCH vice-president for policy, Dr Mike McKean, said: “Vaping is still a relatively new product, and there is much we do not yet know about its long-term impact on children and young people but a clear and concerning picture is emerging.

"Continued research and monitoring essential if we are to properly understand the risks and respond to emerging evidence.”

The smoking and vaping laws explained

‌



A spokesperson for The Children's Society said: "There is a concerning and widespread lack of awareness about what vapes actually contain – both legal and illegal.

"We are increasingly seeing illegal vapes confiscated from children that contain Spice rather than the THC or the cannabis they're sold as. Spice is a powerful synthetic drug that can cause serious effects including dizziness, heart palpitations, and seizures.

"Legal vapes carry risks too. A misunderstanding of how much nicotine they contain can drive heavier use and addiction.

Article continues below

"Childhood vape addiction must be taken seriously, not only because of the health risks but also because dependency can be used to exploit and abuse children."

Hazel Cheeseman, Chief Executive of Action on Smoking and Health said: "The evidence remains clear that vaping is less harmful than smoking but is not risk free. The Government must use the powers in the Tobacco and Vapes Act to swiftly bring forward regulations to restrict the promotion of vapes to children while ensuring that adults who smoke can easily access vapes as a quit aid. As it was with tobacco, strong controls on marketing and promotion will be key to reducing youth vaping.”

News.title: John Lewis reveals top 10 Christmas toys 2026 - featuring wooden play set and dolls house
News.content:
John Lewis reveals top 10 Christmas toys 2026 - featuring wooden play set and dolls house

John Lewis is hailing the joy of the toy box and expects wish lists will be topped with products that encourage loved ones to spend time together

View 4 Images This wooden breakfast set has been named one of John Lewis' top ten toys (Image: John Lewis)

John Lewis has revealed its top ten toys for Christmas - and the high street giant predicts families will ditch screens for play time this festive season.

‌



The retailer is hailing the joy of the toy box and expects wish lists will be topped with products that encourage loved ones to spend time together. A wooden breakfast set and classic dolls house are just some of the toys that have made the cut.

‌



They say it's the most important meal of the day, and the John Lewis Wooden Breakfast in Bed set features a serving tray, toast, croissant, yoghurt and fruit pieces for £24.

‌



The dolls house is based on Paddington the bear - but it comes with a hefty price tag. Le Toy Van Paddington Doll's House is priced at £299.95 and is based on the nation’s favourite bear and the four-storey Brown family home.

View 4 Images Le Toy Van Paddington Doll's House costs £299.95 (Image: John Lewis)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle plan move back to UK in matter of weeks READ MORE :

John Lewis says Marvin’s Magic is set to bring back joyful charm of the classic living room show, with the Marvin's Magic Treasured Tricks Wooden Set, £39.99.

‌



Ever the Christmas classic, popular brands such as Lego are also still expected to triumph this year - with a new Icons 10361 Winter Village Collection Holiday Express Train, £109.99, predicted to be a bestseller.

John Lewis also believes K-Pop to be a continuing trend, with its list also featuring a Rumi Singing Doll for £34.99.

View 4 Images The Connetix Ball Run Launcher costs £45 (Image: John Lewis)

‌



Meanwhile, the Connetix Ball Run Launcher, £45, is an interactive that allows kids to built and swap tube pieces to see how each change transforms the outcome of their run.

Alan Wright, toy expert and buyer at John Lewis, said: “This year’s Top Ten Toys welcome families to put the living room back at the heart of family life. As a nation, we’re witnessing a ‘Great Play Revival’, with ‘playtime’ toys - think those that encourage collaboration, creativity and outdoor adventure - making up nearly half of all sales in the John Lewis toy department.

“Families are actively choosing connection over collection and swapping screen time for shared experiences that create lasting memories.”

Article continues below

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle plan move back to UK in matter of weeks
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle plan move back to UK in matter of weeks

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, are set to return to Britain with Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, for an extended period

View 7 Images Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are pictured at an event this month (Image: The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are planning a major return to Britain – with their two children set to attend school in the UK.

‌



The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are understood to be preparing to return to Britain with Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, for an extended period.

‌



The family is expected to arrive by the end of August, with the children due to begin the new school year in September. The move comes six years after Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties and relocated to the US.

‌



The couple are understood to have secured a private, non-royal home in Britain, although details of their new residence and the children's school have not been disclosed for security and privacy reasons.

View 7 Images King Charles is said to be aware of the plans

King Charles is said to be aware of the plans, with the move potentially giving the monarch more opportunities to spend private time with his grandchildren. Charles and Harry had an emotional reunion last month, which the Mirror told would likely pave the way for Harry's return to the UK.

‌



Despite making millions since leaving his role as a working royal in 2020, and arranging his own private security team, Harry has claimed he remains a target for terrorists in the UK and needs protection from the Metropolitan Police when he returns.

A 40-page risk assessment suggested he faced an “elevated risk” in the UK, where five of the six known terror plots against him originated. At least four individuals responsible for those threats are thought to be out of prison, and their whereabouts are unknown.

View 7 Images Prince Harry shares World Cup pictures of Princess Lilibet and Prince Archie

‌



The Home Office has always maintained that Harry’s security is considered on a case-by-case basis and if he informs the department of his travel plans at least 28 days in advance.

The Duke has spent years challenging the decision over his security arrangements after losing taxpayer-funded protection when he ceased to be a working royal and moved overseas. His return could therefore reignite questions over what security arrangements will be put in place for the Sussexes and who would pay for them.

Harry and Meghan have retained their home in Montecito, California, meaning their reported British move does not necessarily signal a permanent abandonment of their US base.

‌



View 7 Images Before this year, Prince Harry last saw the King in late 2025 (Image: PA)

The return does not mean Harry and Meghan are becoming working royals again. The Sussexes are expected to remain financially independent and continue their commercial and charitable work, while Harry is not expected to undertake official royal duties.

The decision is particularly striking given Harry's previous concerns about bringing his family back to Britain. It comes after it was reported this week that the Prince could return to the UK "every few months".

‌



The report followed the Prince's July return to the UK, during which he met with the King and Queen for a strictly under-wraps visit with his children, and he teed up a battle with the Home Office over his taxpayer-funded security.

View 7 Images Harry and Meghan's children are reportedly starting school in the UK this September (Image: Meghan/Instagram)

The Prince is determined to reconcile with his family and won’t do anything to jeopardise it, a source told the Mirror, as he places far greater importance on repairing family ties than at any point since he and his wife Meghan stepped back as working royals in 2020.

‌



On the cards, the source said, could even be a public reunion with the King at his Invictus Games in Birmingham next year, with the Prince having visited the major city a year ahead of the competition during his visit in July.

They said: "There's no doubt he [Harry] enjoyed his time in the UK with his family, especially getting the opportunity to see his father with his wife and children.

View 7 Images Prince Harry and Meghan with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet (Image: @meghan/Instagram)

‌



"The last few years have been incredibly emotional for him, and now he's reached a place where he wants to not only visit his home country more, but also would really like to be with his family. If the King were to attend the Invictus Games next year, and appear in public with him, it would be a huge moment for all of them. He wants the Birmingham Games to be the best ever, and it would be extra special to have all his family by his side, and that means the King as well.

"He's said before that he would like reconciliation with his family, so undoubtedly he's determined to make things work, and that means not doing anything to jeopardise that."

The Telegraph reports that sources have told them the family will set up their main home in the UK and see how it goes before making any permanent decisions.

‌



Following the news that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex will move back to Britain later this month, a Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK Government’s protective security system is rigorous and proportionate.

View 7 Images The family move will divide opinions (Image: alexilubomirski/Instagram)

It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals’ security.”

Article continues below

The Home Secretary does not get involved in security arrangements for members of the royal family or other key public figures, and decisions are taken by the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures (Ravec).

The committee’s membership includes the Home Office, Metropolitan Police and royal household, who work together to advise the independent chair in making decisions, which are informed by expert risk assessments and in line with Government policy.

News.title: Serial conwoman's massive £67,000 haul pictured for first time as police reveal she stole WW1 medals
News.content:
Serial conwoman's massive £67,000 haul pictured for first time as police reveal she stole WW1 medals

Conwoman Ariana Rose posed as a landlady and house-sitter, and went to great lengths to steal items worth £67,000 from her victims, Southwark Crown Court heard during her trial

View 4 Images Ariana Rose was found to have scanned wealthy clients of their money (Image: Warwickshire Police / SWNS)

A glam conwoman whose arrest was captured on body-cam by officers was sitting on a hoard of stolen goods - including pinched World War One medals and a CBE.

‌



Ariana Rose, 40, who was described in court as a "magpie-like" thief, was jailed for five years in July after she was found to have used a string of fraudulent schemes to scam wealthy victims. She used her ill-gotten gains to fund her own lavish lifestyle.

‌



Southwark Crown Court heard she splashed the money on holidays abroad, luxurious food like lobster and champagne at Claridge's designer clothes and even a Rolex watch before authorities caught on to her schemes.

‌



Family furious as they arrive in Egypt to discover luxury holiday ruined by scam READ MORE :

Woman who hid husband given 465 years to pay back £28k she claimed in benefits READ MORE :

View 4 Images Police discovered a huge haul of stolen items at Rose's property (Image: Warwickshire Police / SWNS)

The court heard that Rose had posed as a house-sitter and a landlady at two properties in Shipston-on-Stour and Southam, in Warwickshire, to fleece her victims of thousands of pounds in cash, and also stole their valuable goods. On top of her Claridge feasting and high-end purchases, she had been driving around in rented BMWs.

Footage now released by Warwickshire Police showed officers approaching Rose as she sat in her car in a car park, with the scammer looking visibly shaken and saying "OK, OK", as she was informed she was under arrest.

‌



Additional videos captured the moment officers discovered stolen war medals and a CBE while searching her property, stolen Christmas ornaments, limited-edition books, and jewellery. One officer reacting to the eclectic haul could be heard saying: "Oh my God, you're joking."

View 4 Images Rose was arrested while in her car at a Warwickshire carpark (Image: Warwickshire Police / SWNS)

In all, Southwark Crown Court heard, her fraud amounted to around £67,000. She was found guilty of five counts of theft from dwelling in December last year and jailed on July 2.

‌



Rose, from Chelsea, London, pleaded guilty to five charges of theft, four fraud offences, four of forgery and one of perverting the course of justice. The court heard Rose went to great lengths to trick her victims before stealing from them, and even prepared a meal and a cake for one of her victims when they returned from holiday.

They later discovered a number of items missing and some had been replaced with fakes. Items taken from both properties included jewellery exceeding the value of £35,000, a Le Creuset Balti pan and a silver dish.

View 4 Images Jewellery and medals were among Rose's haul (Image: Warwickshire Police / SWNS)

Article continues below

When Rose was arrested, officers discovered photos of stolen items from each of the houses she had looked after on her phone. Detective Constable Adam Stather, of Warwickshire Police, said after the case: "Rose lived a lavish lifestyle, funded by the things she stole from her victims who trusted her to look after their homes.

"These items were mostly highly sentimental and cherished. We hope that the victims find some comfort now that she has been caught and held accountable for her actions."

News.title: Met Office identifies 12 areas to face heavy rain on Thursday – see full list
News.content:
Met Office identifies 12 areas to face heavy rain on Thursday – see full list

The Met Office has named 12 areas across England and Scotland set to be hit by heavy rain and thunderstorms on Thursday - and yellow weather warnings are in place

View 3 Images Rain is expected across the UK, including London, on Thursday (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA/Shutterstock)

Downpours will lash across most of the UK on Thursday — and it'll be thundery in places.

‌



Weather maps from the Met Office show the low pressure will sweep southeastwards throughout the day. Rain will be the heaviest across the East of England during the afternoon.

‌



Weather warnings for thunderstorms are in place, issued by the Met Office. One concerns large swathes of northern England, such as Greater Manchester, Merseyside and West Yorkshire, where flooding of homes and businesses is likely. Some short-term loss of power and other services is possible as well, forecasters stress.

‌



Temperatures are falling too. The Met Office recorded a high of 28.6C on Tuesday in Bournemouth, Devon, but 14C is likely in other parts on Thursday. Parts of northern England will see the mercury drop further to around 12C on Friday, meteorologists understand.

UK heatwaves give way to rain for some as Brits welcome relief from scorching temperatures READ MORE :

Met Office names 44 areas facing storms and power cuts with 22 hours of warnings READ MORE :

View 3 Images Met office weather map show areas which will be affected by rain in the early hours of Thursday (Image: Met Office)

The Met Office's forecast for Thursday reads: "Sunny spells and scattered showers. The focus for the heaviest showers will transfer to other areas of England and Wales, with thunder again possible. Feeling cool in the northerly breeze."

‌



The unsettled period follows rain on Wednesday — the first most of the UK had seen in weeks — which came as a welcome relief following the latest heatwave. Photographs show Brits embracing the showers, which finally arrived after a long drought. More than half of England, though, remains in official drought. Last month was in fact the driest July on record for England and Wales, reports the Express.

Southern England has been among the worst affected, registering its driest month since records began in 1836. While the anticipated shift in weather conditions might offer some respite to drought-stricken regions, the Environment Agency has warned that only prolonged and significant rainfall will be sufficient to genuinely improve the circumstances.

But the weekend looks drier, with some spells of sunshine anticipated in the Southeast of England. Sunday is thought to be warmest day, but still quite cooler than last week's 38C high, recorded in Kew, southwest London.

‌

News.title: 'My mum was murdered by her abusive partner — authorities missed the warning signs'
News.content:
'My mum was murdered by her abusive partner — authorities missed the warning signs'

Shaun Hall was 13 when his mum Michaela, then 49, was murdered by Lee Kendall, her ex-con boyfriend whose dozens of previous convictions were well known to police

View 6 Images Shaun Hall witnessed his mum Michaela being violently abused by her ex-con boyfriend (Image: William Dax / SWNS)

A teen whose mum was murdered by her abusive partner when he was a young boy has said there were multiple chances missed to save her.

‌



Shaun Hall watched his mum Michaela being physically and mentally abused by her partner of two years, Lee Kendall. She was subject to physical and mental attacks, which Shaun, now 18, witnessed as a boy, before the mum, aged 49, was stabbed in the eye by the kitchen knife-wielding serial thug in 2021.

‌



He has bravely spoken out five years after her death to criticise police and other authorities involved in her tragic case, saying they had continuously let her down.

‌



Hidden domestic abuse victims given anonymous voice in groundbreaking UK survey READ MORE :

View 6 Images Shaun remembers Michaela as a 'wonderful' mum (Image: William Dax / SWNS)

Shaun said he was shielded from much of the terror inflicted on his mum by Kendal during their brief relationship, with Michaela having moved him out of the family home in Mount Hawke, Cornwall, seven months before her death for his own safety.

She was killed when he was aged just 13 after Kendall stabbed her during a row over a meal she made for him, and after officers sent to her property attended the home without going inside.

‌



Now an adult, Shaun says he is determined to expose the failings in his mum's case and is suing the police and probation service over missed opportunities. They include officers attending Michaela's home on the night of her death left the scene saying she "doesn't help herself", and Kendall's long history of offending.

The thug was well known to cops and had 47 previous convictions across 78 offences and authorities had recorded 16 assaults by him against Hall.

He had only been released from prison for assaulting her two weeks before the fatal attack but moved back in with her after being wrongly classified as just a "medium risk". This was after the probation report failed to include details of his previous violent behaviour against her - including an incident where he had strangled her.

‌



He was released just two weeks before her murder and allowed to move back into her home without close monitoring.

Shaun said if he was properly categorised as high or very high risk, as the probation services have now admitted he should have been, the extra restrictions and protections could have kept him away his mum - and she could still be alive today.

He said Kendall came "in and out" of his home life, that was broken by spells in prison, but he had always felt "uncomfortable" around him.

‌



He said: "The night she was killed police came to the house but did nothing. The police said she 'didn't help herself'. How can you say that to a victim of domestic abuse? She was trapped in the relationship and wanted help. Yet they just left her there without doing anything - and hours later she was dead."

Truro Crown Court had previously heard how Kendall had drunk five bottles of wine and became angry over a dinner that "he didn't want" before he stabbed her to death in the bedroom on May 31, 2021. He was jailed for life and told he would serve a minimum 21 years.

View 6 Images Shaun has criticised failings by police before his mother's murder (Image: William Dax / SWNS)

‌



Speaking for the first time about his mother's murder, Shaun said said there had been numerous call-outs to the home over the abuse, but on the night of the murder police saw no sign of a disturbance and left.

Body-worn camera footage recorded one of the officers talking to the police control room, saying how they had visions of "her lying there with him covering her mouth". She was found dead by her father, Shaun's granddad Peter Hall the following evening.

During that time police attended two further times but did not enter. Michaela's mother then called police for a welfare check but police did not attend so they went to the house themselves.

‌



At an inquest held in 2024, coroner Andrew Cox said there had been "shortcomings and errors" by probation services before her death. Shaun, who now lives with his grandparents near Redruth, Cornwall, said: "I was only 13 at the time so I'm only just been learning what happened.

"But I understand the situation a lot better now and want to speak out now I'm 18. I need to raise awareness to stop a repeat of this happening to anyone else.

"My mum was failed terribly by the police and probation service. We need change to stop this from happening again. The police failed her by not doing more to stop him and from not entering the property the night she was attacked.

‌



"The probation also failed by classifying him as medium risk - he should have been high risk considering his past. All of what we are doing is in her name. I just want to bring justice for my mum.

"I knew mum would also want to do something like this. To help other people - it is what she would have done. I am now using this as motivation to get me through everything." Shaun said his mum met her killer in 2019 while she was doing charity work to help rehome prisoners and get them back on their feet.

He added: "I don't think I was ever fully aware of what he was truly like as a person. He was just in the background. I did not fully understand domestic abuse.

‌



"I knew what was happening but I did not know how I was meant to deal with it or what I was meant to do. We spoke a bit as he was living in the house. I did try and get along with him as mum was dating him. I did not want things to be awkward but I never really got along with him. He did make me feel very uncomfortable."

View 6 Images Shaun said he was spared from watching much of the abuse his mum received (Image: Shaun Hall)

"He was drunk a lot of the time and I witnessed some of the domestic abuse. I think at the time I never fully processed what happened but I remember being upset by it.

‌



"I did not quite realise how bad it was though - and it did not hit me properly until a couple of years later." Shaun said looking back now he realises what a controlling hold he had on her. He added: "Getting into a relationship with him caused her to lose her job. She just went downhill from there.

"At the time I was confused and did not understand what my mum saw in him. He was in and out of prison and went back inside for a year for domestic abuse.

"When he came out he was here most of the time, then would go away back to prison. He was in and out of our lives but mum would always stand by him. But it was a very manipulative relationship. He exerted a lot of control without her realising. It was not just physical but there was a lot of mental abuse and mind games.

‌



"I remember at the time finding it very confusing. They would have a massive row and then it would be completely fine. It was a weird environment."

Following his 18th birthday, Shaun has become much more understanding of what his mum went through, and learned about many of the failings the inquest. He is now working alongside the Good Law Project to hold the authorities to account.

He added: "They are handling the legal side but since I've become an adult I am able to do something about it and that is what drives me to keep fighting.

‌



"I don't think police were fully trained around domestic violence. They were aware of my mum's situation but they didn't understand what it was like to be my mum. One officer said 'she doesn't help herself' which is not how you deal with a victim.

"It was very hard for mum to help herself in a very difficult situation. There needs to be a lot more awareness made around people in that situation among the police."

View 6 Images Among the reasons his mum was failed, Shaun said, was that police lacked domestic violence training (Image: William Dax / SWNS)

‌



"They need to understand what people are going through. She didn't feel she had the ability to leave him." Shaun said they were suing the police and probation service with the intention to put more pressure on authorities to make changes.

He added: "They didn't take it seriously and seriously underplayed the situation. There were obviously multiple incidents of when he could and should have gone back to prison.

"No one made that call. It always felt a bit lazy just to let him back out and wait for something bigger to happen to then lock him away for a longer time. That obviously did happen - but the result of that was my mum lost her life. If he was properly categorised as a high risk the extra restrictions could have kept him away.

‌



"That was another opportunity to prevent this. We have no option but to go down the legal route. It is so important we stop this from happening again."

Shaun said his childhood with his mum before she met Kendall was a happy one. Describing his "wonderful" mum, he said: "She was always very loving. She was a wonderful mum and always made us feel comfortable. She tried her best to make things as nice as possible."

He added: "She was very caring to everyone, close friends and family and would always look out for everyone. Getting involved in that relationship was really out of character for her. But there is not really a certain type of person it happens to. It just shows it can happen to anyone."

‌



Michaela's dad Peter Hall, 74, said the case had proved the probation service was "not fit for purpose."

He added: "It was catastrophic. The mistakes meant he was released as a medium risk with everything that went with that. He should have clearly been a high risk and therefore under much more scrutiny when he was released.

"Had the proper information been given to the judge they would have had more powers to keep him in prison or monitor him more closely upon his release.

‌



"He had tried to strangle my daughter. The woman forgot to put that in her report. When it went to the judge he classed it as he did without the full information and only had certain options."

View 6 Images Shaun said he has become more cognizant of what happened to his mum since turning 18 (Image: William Dax / SWNS)

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said Hall's murder was a "horrific crime" but it would be "inappropriate to comment on live legal proceedings".

‌



Jim Colwell, Deputy Chief Constable for Devon and Cornwall Police, said the force "immediately addressed recommendations made by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC)".

He added: "We recognised some areas of learning in formal admissions within the inquest which have been implemented, and this work continues."

Cat Knight, solicitor at GLP, said: "With one woman killed in the UK every three days, Michaela's tragedy is all too common.

Article continues below

"The criminal justice system is failing women and putting them in danger. It's time for the police and probation service to treat domestic abuse as a threat to life and tackle it with the urgency it demands."

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan moving back to UK
News.content:
The Sussexes and their children visited the King at his Highgrove home in July this year, but it is understood the move was not discussed.

The BBC understands the King was unaware of the move before last weekend but he welcomes the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity.

But there will be no expected change to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Prince William and Princess Catherine have also been informed of their plans.

The couple's move from California comes after they left the UK and royal duties in early 2020.

Family relations had been strained since, with July's visit to the King and Queen Camilla being a key development in their relationship.

The Palace described the meeting at the King's private home in Gloucestershire as a "private family occasion".

It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years.

Prince Harry and Meghan had not been in the UK together since 2022, when they attended the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II.

Security for the couple has long been a point of tension, with the July visit being reconsidered because the duke's request for police protection was rejected.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

The duke had sought to overturn a decision that had downgraded his security after he stopped being a working royal and moved to the US with the Duchess.

News.title: Harry and Meghan are experts in surprise - but is their UK return forever?
News.content:
This has been a relatively sudden decision.

I've now spoken to people who know the couple well. Although there had been general discussions about the possibility of spending more time in the UK, the decision to move back was made recently.

The family's visit to the UK in July was significant.

As well as spending time with the King at Highgrove, Harry, Meghan and their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are said to have loved being with the family of Harry's mother, Diana, Princess of Wales.

The children met their aunts, uncles and cousins. The visit to Europe, which included time in Portugal, where they have a home, was described to me as "such a great time" for the family. It turned a possible move back to the UK into a firm decision.

I am told that this move is not due to any problems in the US. It has been driven by the couple's desire to spend time in Europe, nearer Harry's family and wanting to educate their children in the UK.

Schools have been chosen for Archie and Lilibet. New terms for virtually all schools in England start by the second week of September. The Sussexes will need to settle in so we can expect the family to be back in the UK within the next ten days.

News.title: People smuggler exposed by BBC investigation arrested and charged
News.content:
A convicted people smuggler who was found by the BBC to be living in Leicestershire has been arrested and charged with immigration offences.

Twana Jamal Khdir, an Iraqi national who was once described as "the godfather" of the French migrant camps, previously served a sentence for people smuggling in France.

Last month, the BBC revealed he was now living in the UK.

The BBC has been told he was arrested on Tuesday near Uppingham in a joint operation led by the Midlands Criminal Financial Investigations team, with the support of Leicestershire Police.

He was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service and appeared at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

He pleaded guilty to entering the UK without valid entry clearance, but not guilty to seeking to obtain leave to enter or remain by deceptive means.

He has been remanded in custody and will next appear at Leicester Crown Court on 5 October.

Khdir was given a five-year jail sentence in France in 2016, where authorities described him as one of the most successful people smugglers ever caught.

Prosecutors said the Iraqi Kurd, aged 36 at the time, had earned up to Â£100,000 a week for moving illegal immigrants across the Channel.

News.title: Couple and teenage daughter who died in water off Shoreham named by police
News.content:
Three members of the same family who died after getting into difficulty in the sea off Shoreham have been named by police.

Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, and their 14-year-old daughter Sara El-Khawas are thought to have gone into the water near Shoreham Fort on Tuesday, Sussex Police said.

A younger girl from the same family, who was pulled from the water with them, remains in hospital in a critical condition.

Police said the family had travelled from their London home to visit Shoreham and after reviewing CCTV footage investigators say they believe the deaths were a tragic accident with no third-party involvement.

The Palestinian Forum said the family were British citizens of Palestinian origin, with roots in the Rashidieh refugee camp in Lebanon. Earlier, the Palestinian embassy in London told the BBC that Hassan El-Khawas had been a refugee.

Adnan Hmidan, chairman of the Palestinian Forum in Britain, said the community was "deeply shocked and saddened" by what had happened.

He said two other children were on the shore at the time of the incident.

"Our thoughts and prayers are with the entire family, particularly the children, who are facing an unimaginable loss," he said.

The Palestinian Embassy in London said it was closely monitoring the incident and contacting British authorities to establish the circumstances and check on the condition of the girl in hospital.

A statement issued by the embassy sent condolences to the family and the UK's Palestinian community and wished the girl a speedy recovery.

News.title: Vaccine breakthrough stops cancer returning in trial
News.content:
A new personalised vaccine given in combination with a drug has stopped skin cancer returning in patients during a trial, representing a potentially watershed moment in cancer treatment.

The vaccine, developed by drug companies Merck and Moderna, was given to patients with high-risk melanoma, a type of skin cancer, after they had surgery.

Early results show this new jab extended the length of time these patients were cancer free, but it's unclear for how long, according to an announcement by the two firms.

Cancer experts say this is a breakthrough, but emphasise caution as the full results have not been released or peer-reviewed whereby independent experts examine and check the trial findings.

And even after the trials process has finished, the treatment would still need to be approved by regulators and then go through another approval process before it was made available on the NHS.

The vaccine, called Intismeran, was given in combination with Keytruda, an immunotherapy drug already used in cancer treatment.

Compared with taking the Keytruda on its own, the companies said taking the drug and vaccine together significantly increased the time patients remained cancer free and reduced the risk of the disease spreading to other organs.

The phase three trial involved more than 1,000 patients who had high-risk stage two, three or four melanoma - meaning they ranged from having large tumours in a specific area to cancers which had already spread to other parts of the body.

News.title: Downpours to continue for UK with risk of flash flooding
News.content:
Heavy showers and thunderstorms will continue to affect large swathes of the UK on Thursday, bringing the threat of flooding and travel disruption.

A Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning remains in force across northern England and north Wales until 10:00 BST on Thursday.

The downpours will drift southwards and eastwards during the day, affecting other parts of Wales, the Midlands, East Anglia and southern England.

Drivers are being warned that the return to wet weather could lead to slippery conditions as well as the risk of flooded roads.

Temperatures are also forecast to drop with some places expected to remain below the August average over the next few days.

News.title: Vapes could lead to health harms in children, doctors warn
News.content:
Vaping could lead to health harms in children and young people and should be made "less attractive" to them, doctors have said.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) has reviewed about 81 studies into vaping and said it is linked to higher rates of breathing problems and evidence of harm in babies whose mothers used vapes while pregnant.

The review said vaping should not be seen as a "harmless part of growing up".

The RCPCH is calling on the UK government to go further in its proposals to place new restrictions around the sale of vapes and suggests limiting the number of flavours that are available.

The review into vapes has been published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood. Experts from the college looked at the studies involving health or social outcomes of vaping on children and young people.

It said vaping had an association with problems including wheezing and couching, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

Co-author of the systematic review, Prof Will Carroll, said the evidence showed "clear links" with respiratory symptoms, nicotine dependence and subsequent cigarette smoking.

"We must act to make vaping less attractive and accessible to children," he said.

Vice-president for policy of the RCPCH, Dr Mike McKean, added: "Vaping is still a relatively new product, and there is much we do not yet know about its long-term impact on children and young people but a clear and concerning picture is emerging."

"We need to keep pace with a rapidly evolving market and continue to take action to protect children from nicotine products."

In July, the government launched a 12-week consultation on the appearance, packaging and display of vapes with the aim of reducing the appeal of the products to children.

As part of the new proposals, packs would need to be plain with strict limits on branding and only simple flavour descriptions like "apple" or "cola" used.

Other restrictions would move vapes out of sight in shops, similar to how cigarettes and tobacco are currently sold.

The 100-day consultation follows the recent passing of the Tobacco and Vapes Act,, external which sets out proposals to create the UK's first smoke-free generation.

Children aged 17 or younger now face a lifelong ban on buying cigarettes, since it will be illegal for shops to sell tobacco to anyone born after 1 January 2009.

Dr McKean said the new act was "an important step towards protecting children from nicotine addiction, but it must not be seen as a one-and-done solution".

Prof Carroll said the government needed "to go further and limit the types of flavours available to them as opposed to just their descriptions".

News.title: Giant whales move into Greenland waters as ice disappears
News.content:
Sea ice has been disappearing from East Greenland, allowing giant whales to take advantage and move in to previously inaccessible areas.

That is the conclusion of a decades-long study that has recorded - and filmed - hundreds of the world's biggest whales including humpbacks, minke and fin whales, feeding in ice-free seas along the coast in summer.

None of these marine mammals were historically found here as they have been locked out of the coastal waters by ice. Now, as climate change warms the sea and melts that ice, they have adapted.

Scientists describe the result as seasonal Arctic "feeding frenzies" - part of a major regime shift in the ocean environment along East Greenland.

News.title: Students wait for GCSE and BTec grades as app launches for 750 schools in England
News.content:
Pupils in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive GCSE, BTecs and other Level 2 results on Thursday, with some grades in England available through an app that is rolling out for the first time.

Schools and colleges will distribute grades in person, but from 11:00 BST pupils at more than 750 schools in England will also be able to see their grades on their phones.

Results this year come as the government in England plans to boost technical education and address a growing number of English and Maths GCSE resits.

Last year, 67.4% of all GCSE entries were graded 4/C or above.

News.title: Weekly type 2 diabetes jab could replace daily injections
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of people with type 2 diabetes could get access to a new weekly insulin jab to replace daily injections, reducing the number needed each year by 86%.

Patients still have to wait for the treatment to be approved by the medicines regulator before it is made available on the NHS.

The treatment is said to work as well as daily insulin jabs but only needs to be injected once a week.

The charity Diabetes UK says it will help people manage their condition better, especially those who have extra care needs and who require help to inject every day.

Around 4.7 million people in the UK were living with diabetes in 2024-25, of which roughly 90% had type 2.

The condition means the body can't make enough of a hormone called insulin, or the insulin it makes doesn't work properly - also known as insulin resistance.

Diabetes UK says that around 1 in 4 people with type 2 diabetes takes insulin.

News.title: Male prisons in England and Wales have fewer than 1,800 spaces
News.content:
The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it was building more prisons while exploring early release options and expanding electronic tagging.

The figures come after Prime Minister Andy Burnham made more prisoners exempt from the upcoming early release scheme following backlash from victims.

Burnham came under further pressure after the killers of PC Andrew Harper would still be eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Last week, Burnham said he was "confident" PC Harper's killers could be excluded from the government's early release scheme

On August 3, Burnham said in a written article, external he had "wanted to go even further" but had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

A spokesperson for the MoJ said "public safety will always be our priority".

"We are fast-tracking a plan to keep more of the most serious offenders behind bars, on top of murderers, anyone on life sentences and those in prison for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences who are already blocked from any changes," they said.

"We share the public's anger that these options are even being considered, after we inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse."

News.title: Behaviour guidelines for life in UK published for asylum seekers
News.content:
New behavioural guidance for asylum seekers has been published by the Home Office.

A nine-page booklet covering issues including respect in public, sex and consent, and gender equality, has gone online, with guidance on how laws and customs in the UK may be different from the home country of asylum seekers.

The Conservatives said any asylum seekers breaking UK law should be deported and Reform UK claimed the publication of the document meant the government "knows that they are a menace".

A Home Office spokesman said: "We expect everyone who comes to the UK to abide by our laws. If they do not, they will face consequences, including the refusal of their asylum claim and removal from the UK."

According to the latest Home Office figures, a total of 93,525 people applied for asylum in the UK from April 2025 to March 2026, which was down by 12% on the same period in the previous year.

The booklet sets out how asylum seekers must understand UK law, because the consequences of breaking the law mean "you could get in trouble with the police, lose your asylum support, or it could affect your asylum claim."

A section on gender, external explains that women in the UK have equal rights to men, and do not need the permission from a husband, father, brother or any other man to do things like work, study, travel, or make decisions.

Another section on sex and consent sets out how both people must agree to sex or sexual contact of any kind, and consent cannot be given if someone is asleep, drunk, or unable to respond.

And a section headed Respect in Public outlines how it is not acceptable to whistle or make kissing noises at people on the street, nor "make sexual comments to someone, even if you think it is a compliment".

The guidance also contains contact details for organisations for victims and those seeking help with the issues raised.

The Home Office spokesman added: "Returns of failed asylum seekers have reached their highest level since 2010 under this government."

The latest government figures show nearly 70,000 illegal migrants and foreign criminals have been returned or deported from the UK since Labour came to power in July 2024.

The BBC understands nearly 10,000 foreign criminals, including murderers and rapists, have been removed since the last election â a 36% increase on the previous 21 months.

News.title: Track defect found near derailment site - report
News.content:
A defect was found on railway tracks in East Sussex at the site where a train derailed leaving 30 injured, a report says.

Initial findings from the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) found an "irregularity" with the tracks near Lewes where three carriages tumbled down an embankment last Thursday.

The RAIB, which is continuing to investigate the derailment, said it had received "several reports of rough riding at the location of the derailment from passengers on other trains".

Network Rail and Greater Thameslink Railway, whose Southern Rail train was involved in the crash, said in a joint statement they were "sorry this happened on our railway".

Investigators from the RAIB have said CCTV from a train which passed through the crash site at 14:04 BST showed the "irregularity" with the track geometry just before the point where the train came off the tracks.

The 14:24 service from London Victoria to Eastbourne derailed in the Landport area of Lewes at about 15:54 BST.

The derailment left two people seriously injured, and 18 were taken to hospital with less serious injuries. The 18 have since left hospital.

News.title: Jump in energy bills drives UK inflation to highest rate for four months
News.content:
Higher energy bills drove UK inflation up to 2.9% in the year to July, the highest level in four months, according to new figures.

Gas prices soared at the sharpest pace in almost four years, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, leading to an increase in the cap on household energy bills in July. Energy costs surged after US-Israel war with Iran began, which has restricted global oil supplies.

July's reading is the highest since March but some price growth slowed. Food inflation, at 1.3%, is at its lowest rate for close to five years.

Experts said the inflation figure is unlikely to influence the Bank of England to change its key interest rate at its next meeting in September.

Energy costs for households rose on 1 July after Ofgem, the energy regulator, increased the price cap on gas and electricity costs by 13%, which added Â£221 a year to the typical bill.

Homes are forecast to see a 4% rise in energy bills from October, according to Cornwall Insight, which would take them to the highest level since July 2023.

There is ongoing uncertainty over the US-Iran conflict, which has seen effective closures of the Strait of Hormuz, a key trading passage for ships carrying oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities.

Cornwall Insight, an independent energy consultancy, added that energy price pressures were being compounded by the ongoing heatwave across Europe "increasing gas demand for power generation to meeting air conditioning and cooling demand".

News.title: Two accused of drug trafficking after UK-Nigeria investigation
News.content:
A man and a woman have been charged with international drugs trafficking offences as part of an investigation involving police in the UK and Nigeria.

Oladipupo Atandare, 50, from Dagenham and Latifat Yusuf, 44, from Hornchurch were arrested following the seizure of more than 180kg (397lb) of cocaine in the UK on 5 August.

They appeared at Barkingside Magistrates Court on 8 August and were remanded in custody. They will next appear at Snaresbrook Crown Court on 7 September.

The Metropolitan Police said the arrests related to solely the UK drugs seizure, but inquiries are continuing into the discovery of a similar-sized amount of cocaine in Nigeria.

On Tuesday Nigerian authorities said they had discovered 184.5kg of cocaine, worth about Â£20m, in brown boxes at a courier facility in Lagos.

There have been a series of arrests in Nigeria, including a logistics company employee and a social media influencer with nearly 700,000 followers on Instagram.

News.title: Emma Barnett reveals she 'had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have'
News.content:
BBC presenter Emma Barnett has revealed she had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.

Barnett, 41, returned to Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday morning, explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".

She told listeners: "I made a programme on endometriosis on BBC Two and ended up being in hospital for endometriosis.

"So yes, I've been recuperating, shall we say, from surgery for endometriosis and a hysterectomy to boot. So that's been less fun than the Today programme, but it is lovely to be back."

Barnett's announcement came soon after she published a blog about the "hysterectomy I never wanted to have", external.

The presenter, who has two children, said it was "totally surreal" to be in hospital on the night her documentary was broadcast in June, only well enough to watch the final 10 minutes.

"Some 48 hours before the documentary aired - I had undergone a near-5 hour surgery and somehow found myself lying in bed recovering from extensive endometriosis surgery, a hysterectomy and a gallbladder removal," she wrote.

"Triple threat. Go big or go home. Life imitating art."

She added: "I felt blind-sided and robbed, even though my care had been superb and doctors, utterly brilliant.

"But this was not the road I had envisioned for myself. I had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have."

Endometriosis is where cells similar to those in the lining of the womb grow in other parts of the body, resulting in what Barnett has described as "bone-grinding, life-altering pain". It affects one in 10 women and there is no known cure.

A hysterectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the womb (uterus). A hysterectomy alongside removal of endometriosis can reduce the risk of recurrence, according to Endometriosis UK, external.

In her blog, Barnett also said she suspected most of her pain may have been down to another condition, adenomyosis, which can be treated by a hysterectomy.

Her surgery was necessitated after she had an ultrasound while filming the final scene of the documentary, and a problem in her gallbladder was found. "Suddenly things became urgent and non negotiable."

The broadcaster added that she was hopeful that the surgery had helped.

She wrote: "Early indications are that the pain is very much improved - although I am still healing from the surgery itself so that also feels uncertain and frightening to admit - even to myself."

A verdict is expected Friday in the case of two organizers of an annual Hong Kong vigil to remember the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown who are being tried under a China-imposed national security law that has stifled Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement.

Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, were charged in September 2021 with inciting subversion and face a maximum jail term of 10 years if convicted.

The activists pleaded not guilty when their trial opened in January and are expected to appear in court Friday. If convicted by three government-approved judges, they likely will be sentenced at a later date.

For three decades, the now-disbanded alliance organized the only large-scale, public commemoration in China that attracted tens of thousands annually until the event was banned in 2020 following the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic.

Observers say the activists' prosecution and the disappearance of the vigil symbolized the loss of freedoms that Beijing promised to maintain for 50 years when the former British colony returned to Chinese rule in 1997. The government said its law enforcement actions were evidence-based and strictly in accordance with the law.

Here’s what to know about the case:

Pair organized China’s only large-scale memorial for massacre

The 1989 pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square were one of the biggest challenges to the Communist Party’s rule in China. The government sent tanks into the heart of the capital city and troops opened fire on the student-led demonstrations in a bloody crackdown that killed hundreds, possibly thousands.

The event immediately became an official taboo in mainland China. But the alliance held annual vigils in Hong Kong to keep memories alive across the border until authorities banned the public remembrances during the pandemic, citing risks to public health.

Weeks after the ban, Beijing imposed the national security law that was later used to prosecute Lee, the alliance's former chairperson, and Chow, a former vice chair. Authorities deemed the legislation crucial for Hong Kong’s stability following anti-government protests in 2019.

The alliance voted to disband in the same month as the pair was charged.

Beijing-imposed security law used to charge activists

Many other leading activists are now also jailed under the 2020 law, including the pro-democracy former media tycoon Jimmy Lai. Dozens of other civil society groups also disbanded following its introduction.

In the Lee and Chow trial, prosecutors argued they incited others to use unlawful means to topple China’s fundamental system and central political bodies, including inciting the overthrow of the Communist Party's leadership through calls for “ending one-party rule,” which was one of the alliance’s core demands.

The defense denied they meant to end the party's leadership, arguing the slogan was about moving toward democracy and urging the party not to enforce “dictatorship.” It insisted the alliance had not asked people to adopt any illegal means.

Chow, a barrister who defended herself, cautioned that if the court fails to gatekeep over the reasonable effects of their statements, it could easily become an accomplice by tolerating the crimes committed by those in power.

Albert Ho, their co-defendant and former vigil organizer, earlier entered a guilty plea in a move that typically results in a reduced sentence. His sentencing is pending.

Observers say trial is a bellwether for city's civil rights

The government earlier said all accused have the right to a fair trial and the courts exercise their power independently. But critics consider this case and its result a litmus test of Hong Kong's civil rights and judicial independence.

The existence of the alliance and the city's annual vigil have been considered key characteristics of Hong Kong under China's “one country, two systems” governing framework in the past, said Eric Lai, a senior fellow with the Georgetown Center for Asian Law.

They were symbols of the city's autonomy, Lai said.

He noted the charge of inciting subversion was commonly used in mainland China to criminalize the acts of human rights lawyers, activists and intellectuals, including late Nobel laureate Liu Xiaobo.

“We can see to what extent the court in Hong Kong falls into the level of the party-led judiciary in the mainland through the criminal verdict,” Lai said.

Security officers at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California briefly held five news reporters and two members of the military at gunpoint after mistaking the invited attendees for gatecrashers, according to local news outlets.

The Monday incident took place prior to a private groundbreaking ceremony for a missile operator training facility at the federal airfield close to Santa Barbara. Journalists working for Noozhawk and KEYT were among those detained, with both organizations publishing accounts of what happened.

A spokesperson for Space Launch Delta 30 Public Affairs told Noozhawk that the encounter stemmed from a communication failure.

open image in gallery Officers pointed guns, sirens were sounded, and barricades went up at the gate entrance, KEYT reported ( Matt Hartman via AP )

"Vandenberg Space Force Base is experiencing an increased number of unauthorized entry attempts," the statement said. “When media entered the installation, there was a breakdown in communication and movement continued prior to verification.

"Every potential unauthorized presence must be treated as a legitimate threat until proven otherwise. While we recognize this may have been unsettling, the security of the base and its personnel is our priority."

The reporters and military members were part of a convoy being escorted onto the base by uniformed public affairs staff in a government minivan when they were suddenly ordered out of their vehicles with their hands up, according to news reports.

Officers pointed guns, sirens were sounded, and barricades went up at the gate entrance, KEYT reported.

The two military members assigned to the base — one enlisted and one a junior officer — were handcuffed and placed in base vehicles, while the civilians were ordered to sit on a curb, Noozhawk reported.

The reporters for outlets, including KSBY-TV and the Santa Maria Times/Lompoc Record, were held for more than 30 minutes, causing them to miss the event. All were let go without further incident.

“We respect the military’s need to provide security for the base,” Tom Bolton, Noozhawk's editor-in-chief, said in a statement Wednesday. “But clearly what occurred was unfortunate and unnecessary, and potentially dangerous, as firearms were drawn.”

Bolton said he hopes to have a conversation with base leadership later this week to review what happened in the hopes of preventing a similar occurrence in the future.

Chinese Valentine’s Day is not all about flowers and chocolates. Beyond the romance embraced by some contemporary couples, Qixi is an ancient tradition rooted in legend, prayer and cultural activities that survive to this day.

The festival is observed on the seventh day of the seventh month of the Chinese calendar, which fell on Aug. 19 in 2026. Celebrations are also held in Singapore, Vietnam and other Asian countries.

Beijing’s Folk Custom Museum hosted activities on Wednesday under a program called “Asking for Skills,” reflecting a tradition at the heart of Qixi in which women historically prayed for skillfulness and displayed their abilities through crafts.

“We especially hope that young audiences can understand the meaning of our traditional festivals through interactive and engaging experiences,” said Jia Juan, who works in the museum’s Public Education Department.

The museum, housed in Beijing’s Dongyue Taoist Temple, has been hosting Qixi-related activities for the last 14 years, drawing about 500 people each time.

Old practices become hands-on

Wednesday’s program began with a performance of Chinese classical music, followed by hands-on activities for families inspired by traditional Qixi customs.

One involved dyeing fingernails with garden balsam, a natural pigment traditionally associated with beauty and blessings. Another featured Song brocade bead painting, combining a precious Chinese silk fabric with pearls that symbolize completeness and good fortune.

Participants were encouraged to create their own sachet-shaped Song brocade pearl painting. Their work was meant to embody “qiqiao,” a concept centered on the pursuit of skill and dexterity.

Wang Xuejie attended with her 7-year-old daughter and they created “qiaoguo,” a pastry made by pressing dough into decorative molds.

“We were able to get a general understanding of how, during the Qixi Festival in ancient times, girls and women expressed their aspirations and hopes for their own growth,” Wang said.

A love story in the stars

Jia said that Chinese girls started practicing qiqiao during the Tang and Song dynasties, which spanned the seventh through the 13th centuries.

“The history of the Qixi Festival can be traced back to ancient people’s worship and study of the stars,” she added.

Qixi has historically centered on two main elements. One is related to a legend — its romantic component — and the other to qiqiao.

In Chinese mythology, Zhinü, a weaver girl represented by the Vega star, falls in love with Niulang, a cowherd embodied by the Altair star. Their forbidden love leads the Jade Emperor to decree their separation on opposite sides of the Milky Way. They reunite once a year — on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month — on a bridge formed by magpies.

Jia said records of the Cowherd and Weaver Girl date back to the pre-Qin period, before 221 B.C. Then, during the Han Dynasty, customs related to qiqiao began to develop.

Women carried Qixi abroad

Researcher Lynn Wong is eager to revive the festival in Singapore through an initiative called Qixi Fest, a multiday event launched in 2023. This year’s edition will run through Aug. 23.

“We’re trying to create the childhood memories of this new generation of Singaporeans so that they grow up with the stories that our forefathers grew up with,” Wong said.

She recalls that one day, while talking to a friend about Chinese festivals, she realized she had never heard of Qixi. She then started interviewing elders who shared their memories of the festival. That research is documented in a book.

Qixi came to Singapore around the 1930s with Chinese women migrants. Large numbers of men had previously settled there in search of work, but migration patterns shifted. With the women — particularly those from China’s Guangdong region — came customs and beliefs, some of which faded over time.

“I feel that in my generation, we lost quite a lot of our roots,” Wong said. “I grew up with things like the Tooth Fairy, ‘Hansel and Gretel’ and ‘Three Little Pigs,’ but what about the stories that our foremothers grew up listening to?”

For one family, Qixi endures

Hor Xin Hao, of Cantonese descent, is among a handful of people who preserve a traditional observance of Qixi in Singapore.

Late at night on the sixth day of the seventh lunar month, his family sets up a prayer table facing the night sky in front of his house. They pray past midnight and make offerings to the Seven Maidens, celestial sisters including the Weaver Girl.

Ritual gifts include incense, flowers, perfume, cosmetics and soap, which Hor said are believed to bring beauty and charm after being blessed by the cowherd and seven maidens.

“I personally feel that the idea of a Valentine’s Day actually reduces the original idea behind the festival into something narrower,” said Hor, who sees Qixi as a celebration of traditional values and ancestral legacy.

“It contains the way we look at life from the interaction between us and the universe,” he said.
