The first steel for the underwater stretch of Argentina’s Vaca Muerta oil pipeline has finally left port. A supply vessel loaded 99 pipes at San Antonio Este and set course for Punta Colorada, on the Atlantic coast.

After that short hop, the country’s biggest private energy project starts building the part that touches the sea.

What Actually Left the Dock

The vessel is called the Navvik Launcher, and it is the first of nine platform supply ships booked for this job. Loading began at one in the afternoon on Thursday, August 13, at the port of San Antonio Este.

It carried 99 pipes toward the works area off Sierra Grande, in Rio Negro province. Diario Rio Negro reported on August 19 that the load was complete and the first batch had sailed.

Those 99 are a small slice of a much bigger pile. In June, the bulk carrier MV Athanasia delivered 721 steel pipes to the same port.

They have been stacked there ever since.

Why These Pipes Are Not Ordinary Pipes

Of the 721 tubes, 658 wear a thick concrete jacket. That coating was applied at the Socotherm plant in Escobar, in Buenos Aires province, before the steel went back to the docks.

Concrete does two jobs at once here. It shields the steel from the seabed.

It also adds weight, so the line will not float or shift in the currents of the Golfo San Matias.

The Long Chain Behind One Boat Trip

The pipe itself came from SIAT, the welded-pipe business Tenaris runs in Argentina from Valentin Alsina, near Buenos Aires. More than 10,100 tonnes of it was shipped out of the public wharf at Dock Sud.

Loginter handled storage and stowage at Dock Sud, while Arendal coordinated the sea transport. So a single 99-pipe sailing sits on top of months of mill work, coating and warehousing.

That matters for a country trying to build local supply chains. Because the steel, the coating and the logistics were all Argentine, the project keeps much of its spending at home.

The Vaca Muerta Oil Pipeline in Plain Numbers

The line runs 437 kilometres from Allen, in Rio Negro, to a new terminal at Punta Colorada. YPF has put the total cost of pipeline plus terminal at about US$2.98 billion, which most reports round to US$3 billion.

The buried trunk line is 30 inches across. Near the coast and out under the water, the pipe widens to 38 inches, with 24-inch branches feeding each offshore loading point.

Techint said on August 14 that all 437 kilometres were built, after a pressure test on the Rio Negro crossing. Even so, the wider project was still running at roughly 77 to 80 percent in mid-August.

What Waits at Punta Colorada

The terminal will hold six tanks of 120,000 cubic metres each. Two CALM monobuoys, moored offshore, will let very large crude carriers load without coming alongside a jetty.

The subsea line between the tanks and the buoys is only about five kilometres long. Still, it is the piece that turns a Patagonian pipeline into an export business.

The buoys themselves are built in the United Arab Emirates and shipped out through the Strait of Hormuz. YPF chief executive Horacio Marin said in August that the second unit was already at sea.

The Offshore Fleet Is Assembling

A jack-up platform, the Combifloat C7, took position off Punta Colorada in the second week of August. It will support the work of joining the pipe on the seabed.

Meanwhile the pipelay vessel Seminole is being prepared in Bahia Blanca, after arriving on a semi-submersible heavy-lift ship. Once ready, it will lay the concrete-coated line out to the buoys.

When the First Tanker Sails

YPF told a congressional committee in late July that the first cargo should leave between the end of 2026 and early 2027. Several Argentine outlets now lean toward the early-2027 end of that window.

The system starts at about 180,000 barrels a day. It is designed to climb to 550,000 barrels a day during 2027 and, on company projections, to 700,000 by 2028.

That ramp is the whole point. Vaca Muerta output has outgrown existing export routes.

So a second Atlantic outlet decides how fast Argentina can sell its crude.

Who Owns It and Who Paid

The vehicle, VMOS S.A., groups YPF with Vista, Pan American Energy, Pampa Energia, Chevron, Pluspetrol, Shell, Tecpetrol and Neuquen’s GyP. YPF holds about 30 percent.

Financing leaned on a syndicated loan of roughly US$2 billion from international banks. Argentine reports call it the largest commercial infrastructure credit in the country’s history.

The project is also registered under the RIGI incentive regime for large investments.

The Objection Nobody Has Settled

Not everyone welcomes the terminal. UNESCO has asked Argentina for more environmental information about the works, because of the protected marine area nearby.

The deadline is February 2027. The Golfo San Matias is a calving ground for southern right whales.

Therefore the offshore campaign is being watched closely by conservation groups as well as by traders.

YPF Also Turns to the Younger Sister

While the coast fills with ships, YPF is reviving a very different bet in the far south. Palermo Aike, in Santa Cruz province, is the shale formation Argentine officials call the younger sister of Vaca Muerta.

The province’s first unconventional well, MAYPA. x-1, was drilled by YPF with partner CGC.

It went 3,500 metres down and 1,000 metres sideways, and cost around US$50 million. A production test of about 180 days is under way.

ADNSUR reported on August 15 that YPF is preparing a new exploration campaign there, with work starting in November or December. CGC owner Eduardo Eurnekian has put the play’s potential at up to 10 billion barrels of oil.

He also cites more than 130 trillion cubic feet of gas. Those numbers are company estimates, not certified reserves.

Santa Cruz’s energy minister, Jaime Alvarez, prefers a softer line, calling Palermo Aike possibly half a Vaca Muerta.

What to Watch Next

The next milestones are physical and easy to track. Eight more supply-ship runs will move the rest of the 721 pipes.

Then the Seminole must start laying, and the second monobuoy has to be anchored. Only after those steps does a tanker date become real.

Until then, the finished 437 kilometres of buried steel are a very expensive line waiting on five kilometres of seabed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Vaca Muerta oil pipeline?

It is a 437-kilometre crude line, known as VMOS. It runs from Allen in Rio Negro to a new export terminal at Punta Colorada.

Who supplied the pipes for the offshore section?

SIAT, the Argentine welded-pipe business of Tenaris. More than 10,100 tonnes were shipped from Dock Sud, and 658 of the 721 pipes were concrete-coated at Socotherm in Escobar.

When will Argentina export oil through Punta Colorada?

YPF has guided to a window between late 2026 and early 2027, and recent Argentine reporting leans toward early 2027. The system starts near 180,000 barrels a day.

What is the younger sister of Vaca Muerta?

Palermo Aike, a shale formation in Santa Cruz province. YPF drilled the first unconventional well there with CGC and plans a new exploration campaign starting in November or December 2026.

Sources: Diario Rio Negro; ArgenPorts; GlobalPorts; Techint; Infobae; ADNSUR.

World.title: Argentina Beef Consumption Falls to Its Lowest in Over Two Decades
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The number 46.3 kilos of beef per person a year, measured over the 12 months to July 2026, according to CICCRA.

— The fall down 9.4% from 51.1 kilos a year earlier, or 4.8 kilos less on every plate.

— The supply squeeze domestic beef supply between January and July dropped about 12%, some 163,400 tonnes less than in 2025.

— The price beef cost roughly 52% more in July than a year before, with butcher shops up 56.6%, per IPCVA.

— The bright spots lamb exports rose 34% by volume in the first half, and Panama opened to four Argentine citrus fruits.

Chicken has quietly overtaken beef on the national plate, while lamb exports jump and Panama opens its door to Argentine citrus.

Illustrative photo: an Argentine asado grill with beef cuts, chicken and sausages beside a stack of firewood. Beef consumption has fallen to 46.3 kilos per person a year, the lowest in over two decades. (Photo: Robertaleotta2020, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Argentina beef consumption has slipped to 46.3 kilos per person a year, the lowest reading in more than two decades. That figure covers the 12 months to July 2026 and comes from CICCRA, the country’s meat industry chamber.

Argentines are now eating 4.8 kilos less beef each than they did a year ago.

The Number Behind the Argentina Beef Consumption Slide

CICCRA publishes a rolling 12-month average, so the series smooths out seasonal noise. Its July 2026 reading came in at 46.3 kilos per person, against 51.1 kilos a year earlier.

That is a 9.4% drop, and the chamber called it a historic low. Argentina beef consumption has not been this thin since the early 2000s.

The wider supply picture is starker still. Between January and July, the domestic market absorbed 1.202 million tonnes of beef.

About 12% less than in the same stretch of 2025.

Why the Fall Happened So Fast

Price did most of the work. Beef in the Buenos Aires area cost around 52% more in July 2026 than in July 2025.

According to the IPCVA beef promotion institute. Butcher shops pushed hardest, at 56.6% year on year, while supermarkets rose 43.3%.

Prices did steady over four months, yet the damage to household budgets was already done. Wages have been recovering, but not fast enough to close that gap.

Because beef climbed further than almost anything else in the basket, families simply bought less of it.

Chicken Overtakes Beef on the National Plate

For a country built on the asado, this is the headline shift. Chicken consumption now sits near 49 to 50 kilos per person a year, according to figures from CEPA and industry data.

That puts poultry ahead of beef for the first time in the statistical record. Pork has climbed too, from about 6 kilos per person twenty years ago to roughly 19 kilos today.

The reason is arithmetic, not taste. Chicken prices rose about 30% over the year, barely half the pace of beef, so shoppers switched.

Total meat consumption has held up better than beef alone. Argentines still eat plenty of protein overall, so the change is about which animal, not how much.

Fewer Cattle, Less Meat

Supply tightened as well. Argentina slaughtered 7.09 million head of cattle between January and July 2026, down 9.8% from a year earlier.

Beef output over the same seven months reached 1.689 million tonnes, a 6.8% decline. Producers have been holding back females to rebuild herds, which trims short-term supply.

Carcass weights did rise, softening the blow. Even so, less meat reached the counter while demand for it was already sagging.

Exports Take a Bigger Slice

A shrinking herd is now feeding a growing export book. Shipments between January and July hit 487,200 tonnes carcass equivalent, up 8.8% year on year.

That means roughly 30% of production went abroad, against about a quarter a year earlier. In the first half alone, Argentina sold 280,140 tonnes for about US$2.26 billion.

Analysts expect full-year beef exports above US$3 billion. Since foreign buyers pay in dollars, packers naturally chase them first.

Cheaper Beef Starts Arriving From Brazil

Something unusual is happening at the same time. Argentina, a byword for beef, is importing more of it, mostly from Brazil.

Purchases of Brazilian beef reached about 13,700 tonnes in the first half, up 122% by volume. That is still only around 1.3% of domestic consumption, so the shift is a trend rather than a takeover.

Industry voices describe a slow move toward the Uruguayan model. In short, import cheaper cuts for the home market and send premium local beef overseas.

Lamb Exports Jump 34%

Away from the beef counter, one Argentine meat is booming. Sheep meat exports rose 34% by volume in the first half of 2026, the Agriculture Secretariat reported in mid-August.

Shipments totalled 4,669,757 kilos of product weight, against 3,497,311 kilos a year earlier. Export earnings climbed 46%, and average value per tonne rose 10%.

The European Union remains the main buyer, with Middle Eastern markets growing. Argentina now has 44 open destinations for sheep meat, most of it raised in Patagonia.

Sheep farming remains small next to cattle, yet the growth matters for southern provinces. Santa Cruz and Chubut supply much of the flock behind those shipments.

Panama Opens to Argentine Citrus

The other piece of good news came from Central America. Panama agreed phytosanitary terms for four fresh Argentine citrus fruits in August 2026.

The list covers lemons, mandarins, oranges and grapefruit. Argentina’s Agriculture Secretariat handled the deal through SENASA, its food safety agency, with Panama’s agriculture ministry MIDA.

Panama published the rules as resolutions DNSV 427 to 430 of 2026. Tucumán, the world’s largest lemon producer, stands to gain most, although neither government published a volume target.

What This Means for Visitors and Residents

If you are eating out in Buenos Aires, the steak is still excellent. The difference is what it costs relative to everything else on the menu.

Parrillas have leaned harder on chicken, pork and cheaper cuts. Meanwhile many households now save beef for weekends instead of weekdays.

Restaurant menus tell the same story. Cheaper cuts and chicken dishes have spread, while the premium steaks increasingly target visitors paying in dollars.

What to Watch Next

Two things will decide whether the slide continues. The first is whether real wages keep gaining ground on food prices through the rest of 2026.

The second is the cattle cycle. Once herd rebuilding ends, more animals should reach market, and that extra supply could finally cool prices at the counter.

Imports are the wild card. If Brazilian beef keeps arriving at lower prices, it could put a ceiling on what Argentine butchers can charge.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much beef do Argentines eat now?

About 46.3 kilos per person a year, measured over the 12 months to July 2026. That is 4.8 kilos less than a year earlier, and the lowest figure in more than two decades.

Who publishes the Argentina beef consumption figure?

CICCRA, the Argentine chamber of meat industry and commerce, publishes a monthly report with a rolling 12-month per-capita average. Infobae and other outlets carried the July 2026 reading on 19 August 2026.

Is chicken really more popular than beef in Argentina?

Yes, by volume. Chicken now runs at roughly 49 to 50 kilos per person a year.

Which citrus fruits can Argentina now send to Panama?

Lemons, mandarins, oranges and grapefruit. Panama approved the phytosanitary requirements in resolutions DNSV 427 to 430 of 2026, after talks between SENASA and Panama’s MIDA.

Sources: Infobae; CICCRA; La Nación; IPCVA; Agritotal.

World.title: Argentina Digital Health Plan Lands US$700 Million IDB Credit Line
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The headline number a conditional credit line of up to US$700 million with the Inter-American Development Bank, approved by Decree 757/2026.

— The date the decree was signed on August 18, 2026 and published in Argentina’s official gazette on August 19, 2026.

— The borrower the Argentine Republic, not a state bank; provinces receive the money through individual loans.

— The first loan US$85 million for Mendoza’s public hospital network, with disbursements planned over four years.

— The second loan up to US$60 million approved on August 10, 2026 for Rio Negro, aimed at about 320,000 public-system patients.

The first US$85 million goes to Mendoza, and the province has already warned the cash has not landed yet.

Illustrative photo: the Hospital Central and FUESMEN complex in Mendoza, the province set to receive the first US$85 million loan under the US$700 million credit line. (Photo: Federico Gomez Aghetta, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Argentina Digital Health spending is about to get a large foreign credit line. A presidential decree published on August 19 approves a framework worth up to US$700 million with the Inter-American Development Bank.

The money is meant to drag provincial hospital systems out of paper files and into shared digital records.

What Argentina Actually Signed Off On

Decree 757/2026 approves the model agreement for a conditional credit line numbered AR-O0033. The lender is the Inter-American Development Bank, known in the region as the BID.

The ceiling is US$700 million. However, the decree does not hand over a single cheque, because a conditional credit line works more like an approved overdraft.

Why the Argentina Digital Health Line Is Not One Big Loan

A conditional credit line is an umbrella. Individual loans are then carved out of it, one at a time, each with its own contract and its own conditions.

The umbrella stays open for ten years from the day the agreement takes effect. As a result, provinces can queue up over a decade rather than compete in a single round.

Mendoza Is First in the Queue

The same decree authorises the first individual loan, worth US$85 million, for Mendoza. It funds a project with a very literal name: the Consolidation of the Digital Transformation of the Provincial Health System.

Local reporting says the money will be drawn down over four years and repaid over 25. Interest is tied to SOFR, the dollar benchmark that replaced Libor.

Approved Money Is Not Arrived Money

In mid-August, Mendoza folded the operation into its 2026 budget. Even so, the province spelled out that the accounting entry did not mean the dollars had landed.

That distinction matters across the whole package. Board approval, a decree, a signed contract and an actual disbursement are four different milestones.

And only the first two have clearly happened.

Rio Negro Is Already Second

On August 10, 2026, the bank’s board approved up to US$60 million for Rio Negro. Coverage of the operation describes it as the second project under the same digital health line.

The stated goal is to reach roughly 320,000 people who rely only on the public network. In addition, the loan is set to cover the entire cost of that provincial programme.

What the Money Buys Inside a Hospital

The Argentina Digital Health shopping list is unglamorous and, for patients, quite useful. It covers electronic medical records, appointment systems, laboratory and imaging software, connectivity and cybersecurity.

Telemedicine sits alongside all of that. Because Argentine provinces are enormous and thinly populated in places, a remote consultation can replace a very long drive.

Why Provinces Do the Spending

Argentina runs health care through 24 jurisdictions: 23 provinces plus the city of Buenos Aires. Each one owns its hospitals, hires its staff and buys its own software.

That is why a national credit line has to be sliced into provincial loans. The federal government signs as guarantor, with provincial revenue-sharing transfers standing behind the promise.

Who Borrows, and a Common Mix-Up

The borrower here is the Argentine Republic. The country’s state development bank, BICE, is not a party to this credit line, despite occasional confusion in early summaries.

BICE has been busy with its own peso lending instead, including leasing and small-business facilities announced during 2026. Those programmes are separate from the multilateral loan described in the decree.

Two Other Rule Changes Landed the Same Fortnight

On August 6, the Central Bank issued Communication A 8464. It lets local insurers covering projects under the large-investment incentive regime buy foreign currency to pay reinsurance premiums abroad.

The access is narrow, not general. Insurers must use funds transferred by the project vehicle from its own foreign borrowing, and must act within 72 business hours.

A New Register for Mining Investors

Also published on August 19, Resolution 68/2026 from the Mining Secretariat creates the Mining Investment Registry, or RIM. It replaces the annex of a 2018 resolution and moves filings onto the state’s remote-paperwork platform.

Every beneficiary is identified by tax number, and every declared project gets a unique code. Since the registry also handles single-project vehicles, it links the older mining law to the newer incentive regime.

The Wider Lending Relationship

The health line is not an isolated cheque. In 2026 the bank has also approved US$500 million for Argentina’s targeted energy subsidy system and US$300 million for public administration modernisation.

Those operations follow the same pattern of long tenors and SOFR-linked pricing. Overall, the lender is financing plumbing rather than headline projects, which is slow work and rarely makes front pages.

What to Watch Next

Three things will show whether this is real. First, the signed loan contracts; second, the first disbursement dates; third, which province is chosen third.

Demand for public care is rising. Since the share of Argentines with no union or private health plan has grown in recent years.

Therefore the queue for these provincial loans is unlikely to stay short.

Background: Fintechs and Digital Banks in Brazil 2026: Market Guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Argentina borrowing for digital health?

Up to US$700 million, as a framework credit line with the Inter-American Development Bank. Individual loans are then approved one by one, so the full amount is a ceiling rather than a transfer.

Has any money been paid out yet?

No disbursement has been reported. Mendoza’s US$85 million loan was written into the provincial budget in August 2026.

Is BICE, the state development bank, the borrower?

No. The borrower is the Argentine Republic, and provinces are the beneficiaries. BICE runs its own separate credit programmes and is not part of this agreement.

What will patients notice from the Argentina Digital Health programme?

Mainly shared electronic records, easier appointments and more telemedicine. Rio Negro’s programme alone targets about 320,000 people who depend only on public hospitals and clinics.

Sources: Boletin Oficial de la Republica Argentina; El Cronista; Infobae; El Sol (Mendoza); Devdiscourse; Uxolo.

World.title: Brazil Electoral Fund Frees US$440 Million in Public Campaign Money
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — The release Brazil’s top electoral court freed R$2.3 billion (about US$440 million) on August 18, 2026.

— The trigger the Workers’ Party (PT) dropped its own lawsuit, and the court closed the case without ruling on it.

— The slice that R$2.3 billion is the 48% share split by how many federal deputies each party holds.

— The whole pot the 2026 fund is R$4,961,519,777, roughly US$950 million, shared by 30 parties.

— The clock campaigning began August 16, and parties must pass the cash to candidates by August 30.

The unlocked slice is one piece of a nearly US$950 million pot that taxpayers hand political parties before the October 4 vote.

Brazil Electoral Fund Frees US$440 Million in Public Campaign Money. (Photo internet reproduction)

Money from the Brazil Electoral Fund is moving again. On August 18, 2026, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) released R$2.3 billion, about US$440 million, to political parties.

The payment had been frozen for days because the Workers’ Party (PT) was suing over how its own share was calculated.

What the Brazil Electoral Fund Actually Is

Brazilian campaigns run mostly on public money. Companies were banned from donating in 2015, and Congress replaced them in 2017 with a taxpayer-funded pot.

That pot is the Fundo Especial de Financiamento de Campanha, or FEFC. In English it is simply the Brazil Electoral Fund, and every real inside it comes from the federal budget.

Why the Payment Got Stuck

The court had already published each party’s number on July 1. Yet the biggest chunk of the money never left the account.

On August 13, minister Estela Aranha asked to review the PT case, which paused the judgment. As a result, R$2.3 billion sat frozen for every party, not just the PT.

Other parties could only wait. Because the 48% band is calculated as one block, a dispute over one party’s seat count froze everyone’s transfer.

The Fight Was Over a Single Deputy

The PT did not attack the formula. Instead, it argued that its bench in the Chamber of Deputies should count 69 members rather than 68.

The extra name was Paulão, a PT deputy from Alagoas. He lost his seat after a 2022 vote recount.

Although a May 2026 order from Supreme Court minister Dias Toffoli suspended that process.

How the Court Closed the Case

TSE president Kassio Nunes Marques, who was also the case rapporteur, voted against the party. He held that Toffoli’s order paused the proceeding but did not force a fresh recount.

The PT then withdrew the petition. On August 18 the full court unanimously accepted the withdrawal and shut the case without judging the merits.

There was a second reason to give up. On August 12, Supreme Court minister Cristiano Zanin rejected Paulão’s separate bid to recover his mandate.

How the Cash Is Divided

The split is written into Brazil’s election law and leaves the court almost no discretion. Two percent goes equally to every registered party, so even tiny ones get something.

After that, 35% follows votes cast for the Chamber, 48% follows the number of federal deputies, and 15% follows Senate seats. The 48% band is the piece that was blocked.

Who Takes Home the Most

The Liberal Party (PL), which backs the Bolsonaro camp, leads with roughly R$881.7 million, near US$169 million. The PT follows with about R$615.4 million, or some US$118 million.

União Brasil takes around R$526.2 million (US$101 million), the PSD about R$421 million (US$81 million). And the PP roughly R$417.1 million (US$80 million).

Together those five hold 57.68% of the fund. Small parties are not left empty-handed.

The 2% equal share guarantees each of the 30 registered parties a floor. Although it is a rounding error next to the PL’s total.

What the Money Can Buy

Spending limits were kept at 2022 levels and only adjusted for inflation. A presidential campaign may spend up to R$88.9 million in the first round, close to US$17 million.

A runoff adds R$44.4 million more, near US$8.5 million. Governor races in São Paulo are capped at R$26.6 million, while a federal deputy may spend roughly R$3.2 million, near US$610,000.

Those ceilings cover the obvious costs. Rallies, sound trucks, printed material, marketing teams and paid social media boosts all come out of the same pot.

Why Brazilians Call It the Fundão

Critics use the nickname fundão, meaning the big fund, and the arithmetic explains why. Divided by 158,745,463 registered voters, the fund costs roughly R$31 a head, about US$6.

Lawmakers set the amount themselves. In October 2025, the budget committee lifted the 2026 figure from R$1 billion to R$4.9 billion.

Moving R$2.9 billion away from parliamentary earmarks.

The Argument on the Other Side

Defenders say the alternative was worse. Before 2015, construction giants bankrolled campaigns, and the Lava Jato scandal showed what those favors bought.

Public money is also easier to police. Because the court controls the flow, it can force parties to send at least 30% of the fund to women candidates.

There is a practical argument too. Public funding is traceable, so auditors can follow each transfer instead of chasing hidden company favours.

The Fund Is Shrinking in Real Terms

The headline number looks frozen in time. The FEFC has stayed near R$4.9 billion since 2022, even though prices have climbed since then.

A separate permanent pot, the fundo partidário, adds R$1.43 billion a year for party running costs. That is another US$274 million, paid monthly whether or not there is an election.

Wealthy donors have not disappeared. Individuals may still give up to 10% of their previous year’s income, which keeps a private lane open beside the public one.

What Happens Next

Parties must now hand the money to candidates. The general deadline is August 30, while transfers tied to the quotas for women, Black and Indigenous candidates run to September 8.

Voting is on October 4, with any runoff four weeks later. Since the campaign opened on August 16, the released cash arrives just as television and online advertising begin in earnest.

Leftover money does not stay with the parties. Campaign accounts are audited by the court, and unused public funds must be reported and returned rather than pocketed.

Background: Lula 39%, Flávio Bolsonaro 33% — Brazil’s Race in the July Polls.

Background: Brazil Tax Reform Timeline: Tech Sector Faces 2026 Invoice Shock.

Background: Fintechs and Digital Banks in Brazil 2026: Market Guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much was released and when?

The TSE released R$2.3 billion, about US$440 million, on August 18, 2026. It is the 48% slice of the campaign fund tied to the size of each party’s bench in the Chamber of Deputies.

What was the Workers’ Party suing about?

The PT wanted its Chamber bench counted as 69 deputies instead of 68, which would have lifted its share. It dropped the case, and the court closed it without ruling.

How big is the whole fund?

The 2026 Brazil Electoral Fund totals R$4,961,519,777, roughly US$950 million at R$5.22 to the dollar. Thirty parties share it, and the top five take 57.68%.

Where does the money come from?

The federal budget. Congress sets the amount each year, and the fund exists because the Supreme Court banned corporate donations in 2015.

Sources: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral; Folha de S.Paulo; O Globo; Estadão; CartaCapital.

World.title: Brazil Election Polls: Big Leads in Brasília and São Paulo
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — The Brasília governor race Real Time Big Data puts Celina Leão on 34%, José Roberto Arruda on 22% and Leandro Grass on 18%.

— The Brasília Senate race Michelle Bolsonaro leads on 25%, ahead of Leila Barros on 17%, with Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay tied on 15%.

— The runoff caveat Flávio Bolsonaro 44% to Lula 39% is a Federal District result from 1,600 local voters, not a national poll.

— The São Paulo race Paraná Pesquisas has Governor Tarcísio de Freitas on 50% and Fernando Haddad on 33.8%, a gap of just over 16 points.

— The method Brasília fieldwork ran 14-18 August with a 2-point error margin; São Paulo ran 16-18 August with 2.4 points.

The eye-catching Flavio Bolsonaro lead over Lula comes from Brasília alone, a right-leaning enclave, not from Brazil as a whole.

Illustrative photo: Celina Leão at a Brasília government ceremony handing over police vehicles. She leads the Federal District governor race with 34% in the Real Time Big Data survey of 14-18 August 2026. (Photo: Agência Brasília, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Two fresh Brazil election polls landed this week, and both carry a warning label. In Brasília, Celina Leão leads the race for governor and Michelle Bolsonaro leads for the Senate.

In São Paulo, Governor Tarcísio de Freitas sits on 50%, some 16 points clear of Fernando Haddad.

What the Brasília Poll Found

Real Time Big Data surveyed 1,600 voters in Brazil’s Federal District between 14 and 18 August. Celina Leão, the sitting governor, leads the race to keep her job with 34%.

Former governor José Roberto Arruda follows on 22%, while Leandro Grass of the Workers’ Party takes 18%. Paula Belmonte has 6% and Ricardo Cappelli has 5%.

Blank and spoiled ballots account for 6%, and another 8% of voters are undecided. The margin of error is two percentage points, at 95% confidence.

The Senate Race in the Capital

Michelle Bolsonaro, the former first lady, leads the Senate contest with 25%. This is her first run for office, and she stands for the Liberal Party.

Leila Barros follows on 17%. Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay are tied on 15%, so the fight for the second seat still looks wide open.

The Federal District elects two senators in October. Because voters pick two names, more than one of these candidates can win a seat.

Bia Kicis also runs for the Liberal Party, so the two allies share a base. Erika Kokay, a Workers’ Party veteran, holds the left flank.

Why the 44-39 Runoff Number Is Not National

The same survey also asked about a presidential runoff. Flávio Bolsonaro took 44% against 39% for President Lula, a five-point gap.

However, that question went to the same 1,600 Brasília voters. It is a Federal District result, and it is not a national one.

The distinction matters, because the capital leans well to the right of Brazil as a whole. Reading it as a nationwide verdict would be a mistake.

In the first round in Brasília, the two men are almost level. Lula has 36% and Flávio Bolsonaro has 35%.

How These Brazil Election Polls Compare With National Ones

National Brazil election polls this month tell a different story. Quaest, released on 14 August, had Lula on 43% and Flávio Bolsonaro on 40%.

BTG/Nexus, released three days later, put Lula on 47% and Flávio on 44%. Both gaps sit inside the margin of error, so the national race is effectively tied.

By contrast, the Brasília figure flips the order around. That is what a regional stronghold looks like once you break the numbers down.

Brazil holds a runoff only if nobody wins half the valid votes nationally. Local samples therefore say little about who eventually takes the presidency.

São Paulo: Tarcísio Well Clear of Haddad

Paraná Pesquisas polled 1,680 voters across 80 São Paulo municipalities from 16 to 18 August. Governor Tarcísio de Freitas leads with 50%.

Fernando Haddad, the former finance minister, has 33.8%. The gap is a little over 16 points, and it is far wider than the survey’s error margin.

In a simulated runoff, Tarcísio takes 53% to Haddad’s 36.9%. The margin of error is 2.4 points, and the poll is registered as SP-08913/2026.

Is Tarcísio Running for President?

No. Tarcísio registered with the electoral court as a candidate for re-election as governor of São Paulo. Registrations closed on 15 August, so the field is now fixed.

Despite years of speculation, he is not on the presidential ballot. The Liberal Party’s presidential candidate is Flávio Bolsonaro instead.

His father, Jair Bolsonaro, is ineligible and cannot run this year.

Who Is Celina Leão?

Celina Leão was elected vice-governor in 2022 on Ibaneis Rocha’s ticket. She took the top job on 30 March 2026, after he stepped down to chase a Senate seat.

Ibaneis later abandoned that bid. Celina Leão therefore goes into October as an incumbent with only a few months in the chair.

The Arruda Question

José Roberto Arruda governed the Federal District from 2007 to 2010. He left office during the Caixa de Pandora corruption scandal and was later convicted of administrative misconduct.

His party launched him anyway. Still, the courts have not settled whether the Clean Record law bars him, so his place on the ballot remains uncertain.

How the Two Surveys Were Run

Brazilian pollsters must register each survey with the electoral court before publication. The Brasília study carries registration DF-07849/2026 for the state races.

Its presidential question was filed separately as BR-05423/2026, even though it used the same 1,600 local respondents. Real Time Big Data paid for the work itself.

Paraná Pesquisas also funded its own São Paulo survey. Face-to-face interviews covered 80 municipalities, and the confidence level is 95%.

What Happens Next

Brazilians vote on 4 October, with runoffs on 25 October where no one clears half the valid votes. About 158.7 million voters are registered nationally.

More Brazil election polls will land through September, so these numbers will move. For now, treat the Brasília runoff figure as a local snapshot rather than a national verdict.

The capital holds only a small slice of Brazil’s electorate. Even a landslide there barely moves a national total of 158.7 million registered voters.

Background: Lula 39%, Flávio Bolsonaro 33% — Brazil’s Race in the July Polls.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the 44% to 39% runoff result a national poll?

No. It comes from Real Time Big Data’s survey of 1,600 voters in Brazil’s Federal District only. National polls in August put Lula narrowly ahead of Flávio Bolsonaro.

Is Tarcísio de Freitas running for president in 2026?

No. He registered as a candidate for re-election as governor of São Paulo before the 15 August deadline. Paraná Pesquisas tested him for the governorship, not the presidency.

Who leads the Federal District Senate race?

Michelle Bolsonaro, on 25%. Leila Barros has 17%, while Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay are tied on 15%.

When does Brazil vote?

The first round is on 4 October 2026. Runoffs for president and state governors take place on 25 October 2026.

Sources: Poder360; Metrópoles; R7; UOL; Gazeta do Povo.

World.title: Costa Rica Lawmakers Challenge Sweeping State-Secrecy Order
World.content:
Opposition lawmakers asked Costa Rica’s Constitutional Chamber today to immediately suspend a decree that places broad categories of government security information, including budgets and public contracts, under state secrecy. Lawmakers from the National Liberation Party, Broad Front, Social Christian Unity Party and the Citizen Agenda Coalition filed a constitutional challenge against the Executive Decree.

The filing argues that the decree violates constitutional protections covering the public’s right to request and access government information. It asks the court to suspend the measure while judges determine whether it is constitutional. The lawmakers accept that operational plans, intelligence and other sensitive security information may require protection. Their objection centers on the decree’s wider reach, particularly its coverage of spending, procurement procedures, bids, contracts and administrative decisions.

According to the opposition, those restrictions could prevent journalists, legislators and the public from monitoring how government money is spent. The filing argues that secrecy should remain an exceptional and narrowly justified measure rather than becoming a general rule for government security operations.

The opposition’s challenge joins four earlier cases filed by citizens. As of Monday, the Constitutional Chamber was reviewing the admissibility of three appeals for constitutional protection and one separate constitutional challenge. The latest filing does not automatically suspend the decree. Costa Rican constitutional law generally allows a disputed regulation to remain in effect while judges examine a challenge unless the court orders otherwise.

President Laura Fernández signed the decree on July 27, and it was published in the official La Gaceta newspaper on August 10. The measure covers information connected to the National Public Security Council, the Directorate of Intelligence and National Security, known as DIS, and the government security group called Fuerza Élite.

It also applies to other security and national defense coordination led by the presidency. Protected material includes reports, recordings, meeting minutes, operational plans, command structures, intelligence methods, technological resources and police response strategies. The decree also covers procurement records, including technical studies, offers, contract awards, financing arrangements and the execution of contracts.

Government employees, advisers and private contractors who work with the covered agencies must maintain confidentiality. That obligation continues indefinitely, including after their employment or contractual relationship with the government ends. Fernández has defended the measure, saying publicly available information related to national security will remain accessible. She said the decree is intended to protect information that would be dangerous for criminal organizations to obtain.

The president cited organized-crime strategies and the identities of people or companies hired to conduct polygraph testing as examples of information that could expose officials or contractors to threats. The government has argued that disclosing sensitive information could compromise police operations, endanger officials and interfere with international security cooperation.

Opposition lawmakers say the decree goes much further than protecting active investigations or police tactics. The Constitutional Chamber must now decide whether to accept the latest challenge and whether to grant the requested suspension.

World.title: Costa Rica Highway Project Faces Questions Over Removal of Wildlife Routes
World.content:
An internal audit at Costa Rica’s National Roadway Council (Conavi) has warned that construction work on the Barranca-Limonal highway disrupted natural overhead routes used by wildlife, potentially leaving animals more exposed to traffic. Conavi’s executive director, Mauricio Sojo, disputed the audit’s description of what happened. He said the natural crossings were not deliberately removed but fell during earthmoving work and were later restored.

The warning appears in preventive services report signed on April 14, 2026. It followed a March 5 inspection involving Conavi auditors and the project’s environmental manager. During the visit, the group found that natural overhead wildlife crossings connecting vegetation on opposite sides of the highway had been removed, according to the report.

The affected area was between the Aranjuez River and the main entrance to Judas de Chomes, where crews were cutting trees and clearing the highway right-of-way. The environmental manager told auditors that the design plans available at the construction site did not contain enough information about the crossings.

The report did not specify how many natural crossings were affected or which wildlife species used them. Auditors warned that the loss of those connections could force animals onto the roadway. “Wildlife in the area where the project is being carried out is exposed to the risk of being struck by vehicles,” the report said.

The audit reminded project officials that aerial wildlife crossings must be provided under Costa Rica’s environmental guidelines for wildlife-friendly roads. It also cited the precautionary principle recognized by the Constitutional Chamber, which requires authorities to take preventive action when public works could create environmental harm.

Conavi’s project unit was instructed to coordinate the immediate installation of temporary crossings in the affected areas. Auditors also asked the agency to make sure workers receive complete design plans before similar clearing begins elsewhere. The report identified possible legal, contractual and administrative consequences for Conavi, including sanctions or unfavorable court and administrative decisions. It also warned of potential harm to the agency’s reputation.

Sojo offered a different account when questioned about the findings. He said the natural crossings fell because of construction activity in the area, rather than being intentionally removed, and that temporary connections were subsequently restored. The Conavi director added that permanent wildlife crossings are included in the project’s tender documents and will be built as part of the highway expansion.

The Barranca-Limonal project covers approximately 48 kilometers (30 miles) of the Inter-American Highway North in Puntarenas province. Work resumed in January after more than three years of delays. Public Works and Transport Minister Efraím Zeledón said in July that the expanded highway will include 45 terrestrial and aerial wildlife crossings.

The project also calls for widening the road to four lanes, building or rehabilitating bridges and constructing pedestrian bridges, interchanges and drainage systems. Construction had reached approximately 20% overall completion by late July. The government expects the work to be completed in January 2028.

World.title: Burrell Boom man out on bail after allegedly taking cellphone from friend who was giving him a ride but got stuck in ditch
World.content:
Burrell Boom man out on bail after allegedly taking cellphone from friend who was giving him a ride but got stuck in ditch

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 28-year-old Burrell Boom man is out on bail after being accused of stealing a cellphone from a motorist while he was reportedly assisting him after his vehicle became stuck in a ditch.

Roy Frederick Tillett, a barber and construction worker, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with theft of a black Android cellphone valued at $450, which belonged to a man he knows.

Tillett pleaded not guilty to the charge and denied stealing the phone.

With no objection from the prosecution, the Magistrate granted him bail in the sum of $2,000 plus one surety in the same amount.

As conditions of his bail, Tillett must remain at least 100 yards away from the complainant and must not interfere with him or any other prosecution witnesses.

According to police, the complainant reported that on August 11 he was driving along an unnamed street in Burrell Boom when he picked up Tillett, whom he knew.

The complainant said his vehicle subsequently became stuck in a ditch, prompting him to exit and inspect it. He reportedly left his cellphone between the driver’s and passenger seats while Tillett remained nearby.

The complainant told police that he later asked Tillett to go and purchase something for him. After Tillett left, the complainant noticed that his cellphone was missing.

He reportedly waited for Tillett to return so he could question him about the missing phone, but Tillett did not return.

The man told investigators that no one else had entered his vehicle during that period and subsequently requested court action against Tillett.

Tillett is scheduled to return to court on October 14, 2026.

World.title: Burrell Boom man pleads guilty to possession of cocaine but Judge gives him time served for month already served on remand
World.content:
Burrell Boom man pleads guilty to possession of cocaine but Judge gives him time served for month already served on remand

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Burrell Boom resident who spent nearly a month on remand for possession of 0.13 grams of cocaine walked free from the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday after changing his plea from not guilty to guilty.

Eyon Ramirez, 20, appeared in Court #5 around midday, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug. In sentencing him, the Magistrate took into account the three weeks and six days Ramirez had already spent at the Belize Central Prison and sentenced him to time served.

Ramirez, who had been unable to post bail following his arraignment, expressed relief at being released and said he was happy to be going home. He is expected to celebrate his 21st birthday on Sunday, August 23.

Ramirez was first arraigned on July 24, 2026, following his arrest a day earlier.

According to police, officers conducting motorcycle patrol on Euphrates Avenue near Allenby Street observed Ramirez acting suspiciously and allegedly attempting to evade them. Police said that as officers approached to conduct a search, Ramirez removed a white substance from his pocket and dropped it to the ground before attempting to flee.

Officers reportedly detained Ramirez and recovered the substance, which was later weighed at 0.13 grams and identified as cocaine.

Ramirez was subsequently charged with possession of a controlled drug and remanded to the Belize Central Prison, where he remained until Wednesday’s court appearance.

World.title: Cop accused in Kevin Depaz Caye Caulker murder receives 145 pages of disclosure
World.content:
Cop accused in Kevin Depaz Caye Caulker murder receives 145 pages of disclosure

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police Constable Lionel Rodolfo Urbina, who is on interdiction and remanded on charges stemming from the 2025 stabbing death of 19-year-old Kevin Matthew Depaz on Caye Caulker, returned to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday.

Urbina was brought from the Belize Central Prison under a special security escort and appeared unrepresented in Court #3, where he was provided with 145 pages of disclosure, including seven DVDs containing evidence in the case.

The matter was adjourned to October 21, 2026, when Urbina is expected to appear in the San Pedro Magistrate’s Court for the commencement of his preliminary inquiry. He was further remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Urbina was arraigned on January 22, 2026, on one count of murder in connection with Depaz’s death, as well as two counts of attempted murder and two counts of use of deadly means of harm in relation to injuries allegedly inflicted on Neesean Allen and Julian Canul. Reports identified Urbina as a 20-year-old police constable when he was charged.

The charges arose from a violent altercation on Caye Caulker during the early morning hours of June 30, 2025. Depaz, Allen and Canul became involved in a confrontation with off-duty Police Constables Urbina and Darneak Swasey after an earlier incident near Munchies Fast Food on Luciano Reyes Street. Depaz suffered a stab wound to the abdomen and later died at the Caye Caulker Health Centre, while several others involved in the confrontation were injured.

Following an investigation and directives from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Urbina was charged in January. Swasey was not charged with Depaz’s murder.

Urbina remains on remand awaiting the preliminary inquiry.

World.title: Why Belize keeps speaking on Palestine, the century behind yesterday’s statement
World.content:
Why Belize keeps speaking on Palestine, the century behind yesterday’s statement

By Horace Palacio:

Yesterday, from Belmopan, the Government of Belize issued a statement about violence in a land more than twelve thousand kilometers away. It condemned escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian civilians in the West Bank, called on Israel as the occupying power to protect the population, and reaffirmed that the occupation itself is unlawful and must end.

And somewhere in Belize, somebody read that and asked the honest question. Why does a small country with potholes to fix keep raising its voice about a war on the other side of the world?

Today I will answer that question properly. First the facts of this moment, then the century of history behind them, told fairly, and finally why this quarrel touches Belize far more directly than most Belizeans realize.

Start with what is happening right now, because the numbers are staggering. United Nations officials told the Security Council this month that the West Bank has reached a breaking point. Settler violence stands at the highest levels since UN monitoring began twenty years ago, more than 1,400 documented attacks this year across 260 communities, an average of six attacks every single day, dozens of Palestinians killed, roughly 3,800 driven from their homes in 2026 alone, among them more than a thousand children. UN investigators describe a repeating pattern, an outpost rises beside a Palestinian village, the harassment begins, the wells and grazing lands are cut off, the attacks come, and when the families finally flee, the land is taken. Israeli lives have been lost in this spiral too, and Belize’s statement mourned all civilian victims, as it should.

But none of this began this year. To understand it, you must walk back a century, and you must walk fairly, because this is the story of two peoples and one land, and each carries a wound the other rarely sees.

The Jewish people trace three thousand years of history, faith, and longing to that land, and by the late 1800s, fleeing massacres and hatred across Europe, a movement arose to rebuild a Jewish homeland there. In 1917, Britain, then conquering the region from the Ottomans, promised support for that homeland in a territory whose population was overwhelmingly Palestinian Arab, people rooted in those hills and orchards for countless generations. One land, promised in different ways to two peoples. Nearly everything since flows from that.

Then came the Holocaust, six million Jews murdered in Europe, and with it an unanswerable case for refuge. In 1947 the United Nations voted to partition the land into two states, one Jewish, one Arab. Jewish leaders accepted. Arab leaders rejected what they saw as the carving up of their homeland. War followed. In 1948 Israel declared independence and survived invasion by its neighbors, and in that same war some 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from their homes, a catastrophe they call the Nakba, creating a refugee people whose descendants number in the millions today. One event, two memories, a state born and a homeland lost, both true at once.

The hinge of everything came in 1967. In six days of war, Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza. And here is the plain meaning of the word that fills every news report, occupation. It means the Palestinians of those territories have now lived for nearly sixty years under a military authority they did not elect and cannot vote out, while Israel began moving its own civilians into the captured land, the settlers, whose communities now hold hundreds of thousands of people. International law is not vague here. Moving your population into occupied territory violates the Geneva Conventions, and in July 2024 the International Court of Justice, the world’s highest court, ruled that the occupation and the settlements are unlawful and must end. Belize made formal submissions in that very case, and the court’s opinion is the foundation of yesterday’s statement.

There were moments of hope. In the 1990s, the Oslo Accords brought mutual recognition and a promised path to a Palestinian state beside Israel. That hope bled out through an assassin’s bullet that killed Israel’s peacemaking prime minister, through terror bombings that shattered Israeli buses and cafes, through settlement growth that ate the map faster than negotiators could draw it, and through failed summits and a second uprising. Gaza spiraled into its own tragedy, an Israeli withdrawal, a Hamas takeover, a blockade, and war after war.

Then October 7, 2023. Hamas fighters stormed southern Israel and killed about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and dragged roughly 250 hostages into Gaza, the deadliest single day for Jews since the Holocaust. Israel’s response engulfed Gaza in a war in which Gaza’s health authorities report tens of thousands killed and whole cities pulverized, a war that brought genocide proceedings before the ICJ, a case in which Belize formally moved to intervene last year. A fragile ceasefire finally took hold in late 2025. But while the world watched Gaza, the West Bank burned hotter each year, and that is the fire yesterday’s statement addresses.

Now, Belize’s record, and note something remarkable about it. This is one of the very few foreign policy questions on which red and blue have stood in one line. It was the Barrow government that recognized the State of Palestine in 2011. It was the National Assembly, in 2022, that passed resolutions on the character of the occupation. It was the Briceño government that suspended diplomatic ties with Israel in November 2023 over the bombardment of Gaza, that argued before the world court, that welcomed the 2024 opinion, and that filed to intervene in the genocide case in 2025. Fifteen years, two parties, one consistent voice. Whatever else divides Belmopan, this has not.

Why? Here is the answer, and it sits closer to home than Jerusalem. It sits on our own western border.

Belize is a small nation living beside a larger neighbor that has claimed, in our lifetimes, a vast portion of our territory. We did not answer that claim with an army we do not have. We answered it with law, taking the dispute to the International Court of Justice, the same court, the same law, the same principles now being tested in Palestine. The deepest rule of the modern world order, written in blood after the Second World War, is that territory shall not be acquired by force. That rule is not an abstraction to Belize. That rule is Belize. It is the legal ground beneath every square mile of this country.

So understand what is truly at stake when settlements devour occupied land and the world shrugs. Every time force creates facts and law fails to undo them, the shield that protects every small nation rusts a little more. If occupation can be normalized there, annexation can be normalized anywhere, and the countries that should tremble first are not the great powers. They are the small ones whose only armor is the rulebook. When Belize stands at the United Nations and insists that international law must govern, it is not meddling in a distant quarrel. It is paying the premium on its own insurance policy.

And there is something older than law in it too. We are a people who know what it is to be colonized, to have our land promised over our heads, to win nationhood against the appetite of the powerful. A nation with that memory recognizes the story when it sees it, and loses something of its soul the day it looks away.

Yesterday’s statement called for the protection of all civilians, Israeli and Palestinian alike, and for peace grounded in law, justice, and mutual security, two peoples, two states, side by side. That is not radical. That is the world’s own stated solution, endorsed again by more than 150 nations, waiting only for the courage to enforce it.

Small countries cannot send armies, Belize. We send principles. And in a world where might keeps testing the fence, a small nation’s loudest weapon is its refusal to accept that might makes right.

Yesterday, Belmopan fired that weapon again.

It should never holster it.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Higher light bills as BEL adds 1.5 cents per Kilowatt-hour in August
World.content:
Higher light bills as BEL adds 1.5 cents per Kilowatt-hour in August

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Electricity customers across Belize will pay more on their light bills this month as Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) applies a new Cost of Power Adjustment (COPA) of 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour, following a final ruling by the Public Utilities Commission (PUC).

The adjustment is the first under a new regulatory sandbox introduced by the PUC to monitor BEL’s actual cost of purchasing power. BEL reported that its actual power costs over the past six months were 4.3 cents per kilowatt-hour higher than the reference cost approved by the PUC.

However, customers will not be required to cover the full difference at once.

Under the new system, monthly COPA adjustments are capped at 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour. For August, customers who are not enrolled under the Social Rate will therefore pay an additional 1.5 cents for every kilowatt-hour consumed. The charge will appear separately on electricity bills and is not subject to GST.

The PUC said the adjustment will be reassessed monthly based on verified information provided by BEL, meaning future COPA charges could increase, decrease, remain at zero or result in a rebate.

World.title: International News: Colombia quake losses estimated at $9.6 billion
World.content:
International News: Colombia quake losses estimated at $9.6 billion

By Zoila Palma: Colombia’s President Abelardo De La Espriella has estimated that the economic losses from last week’s powerful earthquake could reach 30 trillion pesos, or approximately $9.6 billion.

The preliminary assessment includes damage to buildings and infrastructure across affected areas, Reuters report.

De La Espriella said around 24.5 trillion pesos in losses were linked to buildings, while another 5.5 trillion pesos involved infrastructure. “Just imagine the scale of the disaster,” the president said.

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake caused widespread damage across western Colombia, including in the major cities of Cali and Pereira.

The disaster has reportedly killed 280 people, injured more than 4,000 and left another 143 people missing.

The earthquake represents the first major crisis facing De La Espriella, who took office only days before the disaster.

World.title: 30th Anniversary of National Pesticide Training & Certification Programme 1996 – 2026
World.content:
30th Anniversary of National Pesticide Training & Certification Programme 1996 – 2026

The Pesticides Control Board (PCB) has been dedicated to training and awareness-raising in pesticide life-cycle management since 1988 when the PCB Secretariat was established, and a nationwide awareness campaign launched in anticipation of the Pesticides Control Act, Chapter 216 of the Laws of Belize, coming into effect. The Pesticides Control Act, which came into effect on 31 December 1988, allowed for the phased implementation of the provisions dealing with the certification of users of restricted use pesticides.

On 17th August 1996, the Certified Users Regulations, S.I. No. 112 of 1996 came into effect. The Regulations require users of Restricted-Use Pesticides to be able to extract information from the label to follow dosage, application and precautionary directions; understand general principles of safe and effective pesticide use, storage and disposal; differentiate pesticides according to use and hazard; accurately and safely prepare the mixture to be applied; calibrate and maintain a knapsack sprayer, and understand responsibilities toward fellow workers and the public.

The Pesticides Control Board (PCB) has been dedicated to training and awareness-raising in pesticide life-cycle management since 1988 when the PCB Secretariat was established, and a nationwide awareness campaign launched The PCB’s National Pesticide Training and Certification Programme was thus launched in 1996, targeting an initial 10,000 farmers for training and certification in the first two years of programme implementation.

The Training and Certification Programme has evolved over the years and is currently implemented by a cadre of five inspectors/trainers. The training modules in pesticide life-cycle management are adaptable to different target groups and training approaches.

The programme is carried out nationally on an ongoing basis, with training sessions carried out routinely at centralized locations, and by request from partners and stakeholders.

From 2020 – 2025, almost 6,000 Certified Applicator licenses were issued to persons who were trained and certified as farm and trade applicators under the PCB’s National Pesticides Training and Certification Programme.

The Pesticides Control Board takes great pride in showcasing its flagship programme and its dedicated team of trainers who continue the legacy of PCB pioneers who laid the foundation for the PCB’s enduring mission in responsible pesticide management.

World.title: International News: Traffic in Strait of Hormuz slows as uncertainty over waterway persists
World.content:
International News: Traffic in Strait of Hormuz slows as uncertainty over waterway persists

By Zoila Palma: Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed today as uncertainty continued over the status of the key waterway following a blockade during the Iran war.

Vessel-tracking data showed that many shipowners remained reluctant to use the strait amid conflicting signals about whether it has fully reopened to shipping, Reuters report.

Kpler data showed that six commodity vessels crossed the strait on Tuesday by 0258 GMT, down from nine the previous day and below the 10-day daily average of 11. The vessels included an empty very large crude carrier that traveled along the Omani side of the waterway, as well as two tankers entering the strait and two medium-range fuel tankers and a post-Panamax vessel exiting.

The uncertainty follows conflicting statements from U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran over the status of the waterway. Trump said Tuesday that no talks were underway with Iran and insisted the Strait of Hormuz was open, while Iran maintained that the waterway remained closed to shipping.

The Strait of Hormuz previously handled about one-fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.

World.title: Jamaica lists 60 public beaches with free access
CXC success
World.content:
Sixteen months after announcing a pilot for its Caribbean Targeted Education Certificate (CTEC) in mathematics to tackle “the perennial under-performance of students” in the subject, the Caribbean Examinations Council (CXC) on Tuesday reported an 88 per cent pass rate among the 2,535 candidates who sat the exam in the May-June 2026 sitting. A total of 2,230 candidates passed.

Dr Wayne Wesley, CXC registrar and chief executive officer, made the disclosure during the live results ceremony from Anguilla, saying the results were proof that the region has “overwhelmingly accepted CTEC”.

“I am pleased indeed, and I am proud to announce that of these 2,535 candidates who wrote CTEC module one in the mathematics pilot examinations, 88 per cent achieved acceptable grades, and across the entire Caribbean only one candidate received the lowest grade. It simply means that most candidates are benefiting from the approach. Measured against a generation in which barely one in three candidates succeed in a typical sitting, this achievement represents a remarkable turnaround,” Wesley said.

Acknowledging, however, that “a module is not a whole subject”, the CXC registrar pointed out that “the full qualification still requires completion of every module at the full standard”.

“But that is precisely what these results demonstrate. When learning is assessed in focused, achievable stages, our students do more than cope; they excel, they engage, persist, and succeed. The May-June mathematics pilot proves that the modular approach works for students, for classrooms, and for the region. This landmark result belongs to the young people who earned it,” Wesley stated.

CTEC, the new qualification which was unveiled by CXC in April 2025, is at the same standard of Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) and Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) and utilises the same syllabus.

“For years in mathematics — the subject that is foundational to every vocation in life — only about a third of our candidates have achieved acceptable grades in a typical sitting. Behind that statistic are hundreds of thousands of young people who sat in our classrooms for five years and walked away with nothing in hand to show for what they did learn. Not because they learn nothing, but because our instrument of assessment was an all-or-nothing event. One subject, one sitting, one verdict. If the verdict went against you, the system did not recognise you and stayed silent about your progress,” Wesley noted in explaining the motivation behind CTEC.

“I described CTEC as a game-changer, and I promised then that we are witnessing the beginning of the end of the Caribbean Examinations Council as we know it. Today we keep that promise and we make history in Anguilla by announcing that the achievement of the highly successful CTEC pilot in mathematics in the May/June 2026 examinations and, with the approval of our board of governors, CXC is pleased to officially launch the Caribbean Targeted Education Certificate,” the CEO said.

“At CXC we hold to the position that competence is competence, no matter how long it takes to achieve and no matter how the route and… no matter the route by which it comes. This is how things and times have changed. This is how we have to meet this generation of learners where they are,” he added.

Wesley contended that “an assessment model built in the [20th] century cannot be expected to adequately serve a 21st century generation”, but said “CTEC is assessment redesigned for learners without lowering by a single degree the standard to which we hold”.

“When we were designing CTEC we asked ourselves, would the region embrace it? Today we have proof of concept from a region that has overwhelmingly accepted CTEC. When we invited the region to pilot CTEC mathematics module 1, more than 2,500 candidates stepped forward as pioneers across 15 territories, and 42 centres from Jamaica to Belize, from Barbados to the Cayman Islands and Anguilla, which was among the first countries to sign on to the pilot. Principals told us that their students were excited about the pilot examinations,” he said.

Wesley said the modularised examination format will now be applied to four other subject areas going forward, given the success of the maths module pilot.

“This is a new day for our Caribbean learners on the strength of this CTEC mathematics pilot. The Caribbean Examinations Council is declaring to our students this simple truth: What you know counts. We hear you. We see you. Your learning has been seen, measured, and certified. You are not at the end of the road. You are on your way up the staircase,” he said.

Telling policymakers across the region that “CTEC is yours to embed in your national education strategies, in your workforce and TVET planning and second chance programmes”, Wesley said CXC’s team was ready to work with the various ministries of education across the region and will be visiting territories in the weeks ahead to do exactly that.

CXC also said the 2,535 candidates who were involved in the pilot will continue to enjoy doing the other modules free of cost.

The candidates have a four-year period to complete it and will receive CSEC certification at the end.

World.title: Saving Moo Moo
World.content:
Nicholas Thomas, a resident of Spanish Town, feeds the cow he affectionately calls Moo Moo. (Photo: Napthali Junior)

Driving along Walks Road in Spanish Town, in the vicinity of Crescent Primary School, motorists may have noticed a cow lying motionless on the side of the road in the blazing sun, in the same spot for days. That cow is affectionately called Moo Moo by community members who have been taking care of her since she was injured in an accident more than a week ago.

When the Jamaica Observer visited the area Monday, police officers were seen feeding the injured cow grass and offering her water as community members looked on. Moo Moo ate slowly, pausing between bites as she gulped down water from a Dutch pot, seemingly desperate to rehydrate after days exposed to the summer heat. She remained largely immobile with most of her legs tucked beneath her body as though to protect them from further harm.

Reports from the policemen, Constable Dwight Lewis and Leighton Taylor, are that they were passing the area on Monday when they saw the cow and stopped. Moo Moo is believed to be pregnant and was injured during a hit-and-run accident. The owner has not yet come forward, and the accident has not been reported.

In the meantime, residents have stepped in.

A registered nurse who frequents the area, Gabriel Hamilton, said she spotted the cow about a week ago and became concerned when she noticed the animal was immobile.

“I came into the community, and I was asking around. People were not sure whose animal it is. I got closer to her, and I realised that her front right leg was injured, and I saw some blood in her abdominal area as well. The members of the community also told me that she’s pregnant, and I was like, ‘No, this cannot be’,” said Hamilton, visibly distressed as she recounted the interaction.

An animal lover who almost pursed a career as a veterinarian, she said she immediately sprang into action, calling Hope Zoo, the Jamaica Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (JSPCA), the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) and even her friend who is a trained veterinarian. Members of the community said they also made several calls to animal-related facilities, but no one has come to help.

Determined to ensure that the animal survived, Hamilton said she and other members of the community formed a pact to take care of Moo Moo. She said she entrusted community member Nicholas Thomas to be the cow’s primary caregiver, promising to compensate him for his efforts to keep Moo Moo alive. She had noticed that Moo Moo had lost weight and she was concerned about her nutrition.

Thomas said he was happy to officially take on the role, noting that he was already providing some level of care to the animal.

“When she ready for food she say, ‘Moo, moo’ and so I call her the name Moo Moo and she just accept everything with love,” he said, laughing.

He then bent down to rub the cow’s head, later jumping with joy as he thanked the news team for stopping by to highlight the story. He said he is optimistic that Moo Moo will survive, urging anyone who can help to do so.

Constable Lewis said he has reported the incident to his supervisor, and they are working to get a member of the agriculture team on location to transport the cow and get it medical attention.

“It’s part of our duty to serve, protect, and reassure, so we are reassuring the cow that help is on the way, and we are trying to get through to see if there is any owner so the owner can come and get her. The owner might not be sure as to its whereabouts. The owner might realise that the cow is not back, but as to the actual location of the cow, the owner might not be sure, so with the help of the media, probably the owner can get in touch and then speak to the Spanish Town police,” Constable Lewis told the Observer.

Constable Taylor, who farms as a hobby, said he loves animals and had to stop to help Moo Moo.

“We just want to make sure that she stays alive until the relevant persons come. We wish we could give her some shelter, but it’s out of our hands because we can’t even lift her up, so we just a try we best to make sure she stays alive,” said Taylor.

“Everybody who is passing can give a hand because we can’t stay here the whole day with her, but each person that is passing can give an eye. I realise a lot of persons help out because we come here and see a pot with water, so that’s good. It could’ve been my animal, so it’s good to see everybody helping out,” added Taylor.

World.title: RECOVERY AHEAD OF SCHEDULE
World.content:
JAMAICA could return to pre-Hurricane Melissa levels of economic output as early as the April-to-June quarter of 2027, significantly sooner than previously expected as the year-on-year contraction in the economy narrows and reconstruction gathers momentum.

The Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) said Tuesday that the current trajectory suggests the economy could regain the level of output recorded before Melissa within 1.5 to two years of the hurricane, compared with an earlier expectation that recovery would take about three years and extend into fiscal year 2028/29.

“Note, however, that full recovery — to include rebuilding efforts and replacing housing stock, public infrastructure and livelihoods — will be over a more extended period, possibly three to five years,” PIOJ Director General Dr Wayne Henry said at the institute’s quarterly economic briefing.

The improved outlook comes even as preliminary PIOJ estimates show that real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted 2.9 per cent in the April-to-June quarter compared with the corresponding period of 2025, marking a third-consecutive quarter of year-on-year decline.

The economy contracted 7.1 per cent year on year in the October-to-December 2025 quarter and 4.1 per cent year on year in January-March 2026.

The PIOJ, however, rejected suggestions that Jamaica is in a recession, pointing instead to the sequential improvement in economic activity following the hurricane-induced collapse in the final quarter of 2025.

“Yes, we can confirm that there is not a recession. We are not in a recession,” Senior director of the PIOJ’s Economic Planning and Research Division James Stewart told the Jamaica Observer.

Stewart said a recession also appeared unlikely for the remainder of the year.

While output in the first quarter of 2026 remained below the corresponding period a year earlier, seasonally adjusted real value added an increased 3.3 per cent compared with the hurricane-hit October-to-December quarter.

“Following three consecutive quarters of quarter-over-quarter growth during the first nine months of 2025 the economy experienced a sharp setback in the October-December 2025 quarter as Hurricane Melissa triggered a 7.3 per cent decline in real value added relative to July-September 2025,” Henry said.

“Importantly, the latest GDP release from Statin [Statistical Institute of Jamaica] confirms that the economy has begun to recover from the shock. The seasonally adjusted real value added for January-March 2026 increased by 3.3 per cent compared with the October-December 2025 quarter, signalling a rebound in economic activity,” he added.

The PIOJ, in its latest review of economic performance, said the April-to-June downturn largely reflected the lingering effects of Hurricane Melissa, which disrupted production, employment, domestic demand, and business and consumer confidence.

During the review quarter the goods-producing industry declined by an estimated 6.4 per cent as key sub-industries, including agriculture and mining and quarrying, recorded significant contractions.

Agriculture fell 17 per cent as hurricane damage across major crop-producing parishes was compounded by drought conditions associated with the El Niño phenomenon.

Mining and quarrying, on the other hand, contracted by 23.9 per cent, largely due to a 30.8 per cent decline in aluminium production as technical challenges linked to hurricane damage continued to weigh on operations.

There were, however, signs of resilience in other productive activities as manufacturing grew by an estimated one per cent while construction expanded 0.3 per cent, supported by higher civil engineering activity.

The services industry contracted by 1.7 per cent, with most industries declining. The exceptions were financial and insurance activities, up 1.9 per cent; wholesale and retail trade, repair of motor vehicles, and installation of machinery and equipment (WRTRIM), up 0.2 per cent; and public administration and defence, up 0.1 per cent.

Accommodation and food service activities, one of the larger service industries, however fell 12.2 per cent, reflecting weaker tourism activity. Preliminary data show stopover arrivals for April and May falling 19.6 per cent to 382,745 visitors, while visitor expenditure declined 17 per cent to US$578 million.

For the January to June period or first half of the calendar year real GDP is estimated to have contracted by 3.5 per cent, with the goods-producing industry down 6.8 per cent and services down 2.4 per cent.

Despite the weaker headline numbers, PIOJ Director General Dr Wayne Henry said the underlying trend points to an economy recovering from a significant one-off shock rather than entering a prolonged downturn.

Henry also pointed to developments in the labour market as another positive indicator, saying the pace of recovery reflects the resilience of Jamaica’s underlying economic fundamentals despite widespread disruption caused by the hurricane.

The PIOJ, while maintaining a negative short-term outlook, said it expects the rate of contraction to narrow as more industries recover. The institute forecasts a contraction of 0.5 per cent to 1.5 per cent in the current July-to-September quarter, followed by growth of one per cent to three per cent for fiscal year 2026/27.
