World.title: Pacific Mini Games safeguarding initiative uncovers 11 abuse cases
World.content:
Eleven "safeguarding" cases, ranging from bullying to sexual harrasement, were officially recorded at last year's Pacific Mini Games in Palau.

The cases were reported to the Team Up 'Safe Games' team that was despatched to the event before, during and after the Games.

This was revealed by Team Up safeguarding advisor Roshika Deo in an interview with RNZ Pacific.

Deo said there could have been more cases that were unreported.

The eleven cases were part of the 16 initially reported to the Safe Games team on the ground, which was the first time that safeguarding was integrated at a Pacific Games event.

"It was systemised and it was incorporated pre and during the [Mini] Games, and we were also quite surprised to see that we received 16 incidents that were reported to the Safe Games team," she said.

"Eleven were safeguarding issues and they ranged from things like sexual harassment, physical abuse, neglect and failure of duty of care, harassment and bullying."

Palau hosted the 12th Pacific Mini Games in Koror from 29 June to 9 July last year, bringing together more than 1500 athletes from 23 Pacific nations and territories.

Deo said 70 percent of the victims were girls and women, while 70 percent of the perpetrators were boys and men.

Around 30 percent of the victims were minors and 55 percent of the people affected were athletes.

"So, it was not all athletes that were affected or were harmed, but there were other people involved within the sports ecosystem during the Games that were affected," Deo said.

"But 55 percent of the people affected were athletes and there could have been more.

"This was the first time, so it takes a while for people to build their trust and confidence in a new system."

She said the Team Up project, supported by the Australian government, would continue to create awareness as the work to incorporate safeguarding in major sporting tournaments in the region continues.

They have teamed up with the International Olympic Committee (IOC), UN Women, the Oceania National Olympic Committee (ONOC), Equity Commission, and the Oceania Impact Network.

The programme works to attract and retain women, girls and people with a disability, as well as men and boys; ensure sport organisations are safe, inclusive and accessible; and sport is used to strengthen relationships and build closer collaboration.

Deo said the initiaitve involves more than 35 partners from 15 sports, including athletics, Australian rules football, basketball, badminton, cricket, football, gymnastics, hockey, netball, rugby league, rugby union, surfing, swimming, table tennis and volleyball.

She said sports should be safe "for all, children, adults and young adults".

"Everyone should feel safe, should feel respected and should feel included in sports.

"It's a fun, empowering and great thing to be involved in and engaged in. And people should be able to do it safely, and parents should also be able to feel confident, you know, and secure when they send the children to support.

"And having proper safeguarding measures in place also means you increase the credibility of the sports right when parents, when guardians, when other people see that this sports organisation is creating safeguarding awareness, recognises that these things are harmful and abusive and are doing things about it and has a reporting mechanism."

She said parents also felt more confident to send their children to those kind of sports because they know that they will be protected and looked after.

She said there are so many different kinds of emotional abuse and verbal abuse that happens.

International federations are also taking responsibility and stepping up and ensuring that safeguarding is embedded within the coaching courses that within the different kinds of courses that they offer to people within the sports.

Team Up currently works with seven Pacific Island countries in Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Nauru, Tonga and Samoa.

A major development has been the recent launch of the Safeguarding at Major Sporting Events Toolkit.

World.title: Financial Markets Authority head Samantha Barrass seeks to overturn suspension
World.content:
The suspended chief executive of the Financial Markets Authority will appear before the Employment Relations Authority next month, seeking to be reinstated in her role.

Authority chief executive Samantha Barrass - who had already announced plans to depart - went on leave last month after the authority's board became aware of "cultural concerns" at the country's financial markets regulator.

Days later, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment announced it had started an investigation into workplace conduct and culture at the authority.

Lawyer Stephen Langton, who is acting for Barrass, said she considered her suspension to be unjustified and was seeking an urgent determination from the Employment Relations Authority (ERA) to overturn her suspension and be reinstated to her role at the authority.

"Ms Barrass looks forward to the opportunity to set out her position publicly at an ERA hearing in the very near future."

A hearing date has been set for mid-September.

Last week, it was announced that the Financial Markets Authority board had commissioned an independent employment investigation "concerning matters relating to" Barrass, with Paul Wicks KC to lead the investigation.

The investigation was separate from the conduct and culture review being undertaken by the ministry.

The authority declined to comment on Barrass's move to seek reinstatement in her role.

In July, the New Zealand Shareholders' Association said it was aware of "systemic cultural issues" at the Financial Markets Authority, and believes leadership departures and allegations of poor workplace culture have knocked confidence in the agency.

World.title: Raiders and Broncos are still reckoning with the legacy of a classic
World.content:
There are some defeats so cruel a team cannot survive even if it doesn't kill them and some triumphs that never leave a team even if they go on to greater glories and sometimes, if we're lucky, both things happen at the same time.

That's what Canberra and Brisbane are both reckoning with ahead of their match tomorrow night, the first meeting for the two clubs since last year's double-extra time semi-final that ended with Broncos winning 29-28 in the 94th minute.

It's scheduling malpractice on the NRL's part that we've had to wait so long for a sequel, which now has a direct-to-video quality when it could have been a blockbuster.

Walsh grabs the Sun to light up Brisbane's season Brisbane and Canberra went to the great beyond in their golden point finals match and it was Reece Walsh who led the Broncos to the promised land.

Perhaps they hoped this match would have finals implications but history didn't say it was likely.

Canberra and Brisbane are two of the NRL's great boomtowns — the Raiders haven't made the top four in consecutive seasons in 30 years and the Broncos haven't done it in 20.

Each club has spent 2026 trying to come to terms with what happened to them, both on that day and since, and both have struggled to carry the weight of what came next.

It was match where Canberra's wave broke and broke hard just as Brisbane's was beginning to crest.

That crest became a tsunami in the weeks to come, as part of a series of matches that can stand equal with any in NRL history.

The Raiders win was their greatest escape, as they came from 16-points down with 15 minutes remaining in a game that defied belief even as it was happening.

The Panthers win in the preliminary final was their most cathartic as they exorcised the demons of their 2023 grand final loss with their best all-round performance of the finals.

The win over Melbourne in the decider was their most glorious, capping as astounding a run to paradise as any team has ever had. They will almost certainly win more grand finals in the future but they will definitely never win one like that again.

After a 20-year drought, it was the premiership of a lifetime, great enough that even a fanbase as varied, voracious and expectant as the Broncos was able to forgive their rough start to life as champions.

But a start was all they could forgive because they cannot forget. Their eyes had seen the glory and the coming of Reece Walsh and they basked in the memories of Brisbane reaching a level of brilliance, ferocity and belief that made them a terrible and wonderful sight to behold.

Brisbane finished off the run of a lifetime to win the 2025 premiership. (AAP: Mark Evans)

Such play would never be sustainable over a full season because you cannot spring your way through a marathon, but in 2026 they've barely got out of a jog and the turn against them has been harsh, swift and brutal.

A spate of injuries in the early part of the season exposed the top-heavy nature of their roster and despite a few brave efforts to start they eventually tipped right over and head to Canberra with 12 losses in their last 13 games.

Old heads like Ben Hunt and Adam Reynolds look like they went on a year too long and younger ones, like Ezra Mam, have shown the ability to replace them but not the maturity or consistency.

After a year where he went from a train and trial deal to playing Test and Origin football and the winning try-scorer in the grand final, Gehamet Shibasaki has looked a lot more like the journeyman he was than the premiership hero he became.

The departing Payne Haas has been strong but not the superhuman we have come to know and with him leaving for Souths and Reynolds retiring it will be a new look Bronco next year — maybe for better, maybe for worse but certainly for different.

It has been a listless premiership defence from the Broncos. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

It's clear that victory has defeated them in a way Canberra, Penrith and Melbourne never could. The merciless march of time is a forever war, but for Brisbane the guns fell silent because they had no more worlds left to conquer.

That has brought them here, where the chance of going from premiers to wooden spooners is somehow possible which is made all the more maddening because the qualities they showed in that golden September still lurk within even if they rarely show themselves.

That sole win in their last 13 starts was against the might of Penrith, away, on a waterlogged track they wouldn't let racehorses run on with Walsh again leading the way.

It has been a difficult and stop-start season for their fullback, who has a boundless energy that is sometimes too great for concentration to control.

His struggles was best typified by his last act for the year — Walsh threw a pass that was intercepted and taken the length of the field by Alofiana Khan-Pereira for a try, but only because he battled hard to get into position despite suffering a serious ankle injury only moments before, one which ended his season prematurely.

Losing Walsh means the remote possibility of Brisbane going from first to last must be entertained. This is a team who have been waiting for this season to end for some time now and they are heavy outsiders for Friday against a Canberra team who have plenty to play for.

The reason for the Raiders motivation is not so much their finals hopes, which are desolate enough they're relying on Wests Tigers to win another game, but because of the home farewell to Josh Papali'i, the club's most capped player and modern day favourite son.

It will give the Raiders a north star to aim for, something Brisbane stopped looking for a while ago.

The visitors are waiting for this season to end while the home side wish it could keep going — Simi Sasagi, their best player this year, has a tenderised shoulder but has kept playing because he wanted to suit up with Papali'i as many times as he could.

Canberra will mark Josh Papali'i's final home match on Friday night. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The veteran prop is the best player the Raiders have ever had who has not won a premiership and as a shining example that greatness can be possible in Canberra he's an important symbol for a team that has to continually prove itself to sceptical outsiders.

His achievements mean Papali'i is a living piece of club history and blood and tears will mix together to make it a sentimental day, as so many days are for Canberra because this a club that rides their emotions like no other.

After a difficult season, which began in the shadow of the finals loss to Brisbane and the defeat to Cronulla which followed, this is a retreat into their own hearts and that's the place they always feel strongest.

Last year, their premiership hopes could not have been more brutally buried unless Brisbane had thrown them a shovel, pulled out a gun and told the Raiders to start digging.

That bled into 2026 as Canberra took a long journey from minor premiers last year to second last a few months ago before settling back into the middle of the pack they know so well but after last year it was hard not to want for more.

Canberra have failed to match last year's minor premiership victory. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

This is a team with the second-longest premiership drought in the league and chances to end it are hard to come by.

It has given this year a lost quality, typified by the "self-entitled and undisciplined" football that Ricky Stuart believes cost them at the start of the season, when they fell into a four-match losing streak from which their finals chances never really recovered.

Throw in the loss of Jamal Fogarty, his replacement Ethan Sanders going through the peaks of valleys so many young halfbacks must endure, an injury run that seemed restricted solely to second rowers and a serious ill-suitedness to the set restart madness that engulfed the early parts of the year and it became overwhelming.

Their fall has not been as hard as Brisbane's but neither is it from such a towering height, which paradoxically increases the pain instead of softening the blow. The Broncos, at least, have what came after that day in the capital.

The Raiders have more to play for than the Broncos on Friday night. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

There's a chance that being up 28-12 with 15 minutes left, or the stolen moments before the full-time siren penalty that allowed Walsh to level the scores is as good as it gets for Canberra for a while.

That, like the seconds before Jamal Fogarty's extra time try was correctly chalked off the board even as Channel Nine had literally started the countdown to cut to the overdue 6pm news with the club's song ringing through the stadium, erroneously heralding a victory which never arrived, could be as close as they'll come to the promised land for some time.

A win against the Broncos tomorrow won't exorcise those demons any more than a loss would compound them. The blood is still on the blade but it has dried. What came before hangs over the match, but enough time has passed that it does not loom.

Canberra will celebrate the past as Brisbane wait for the future to arrive and both will continue to grapple with the legacy of a game that reaches far beyond one autumn afternoon.

Both teams, to some extent, have set themselves on fire as they tried to pass the torch from then to now and in different ways they are still running on it's fumes even a year later.

For the Broncos it is intoxicating in a way they'll always remember. For the Raiders it's just toxic in a way they cannot forget.

They are both of them haunted, one by what was and one by what might have been.

World.title: 'Fair bit of anger across the whole AFLW' after Swans players allegation
World.content:
As the fallout continues with focus on the Sydney Swans men's AFL team, the club's women's team has been thrust into an unfair spotlight and become another unwilling casualty.

This was a week when the Swans AFLW team was given equal billing to the men's team with a double-header on the SCG, at a club that is very public in celebrating its inclusive values.

Swans players issue apology Five Sydney Swans players stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards issue an apology.

Instead, the club's respect for women has been brought into question, with the women's players and women in the football community left feeling hurt and angry by the actions of the men's players.

The club has suspended five of its men's players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — for the remainder of the 2026 season for breaching club behavioural standards.

The five players are linked to an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, where the Swans were staying after their win over Essendon on Sunday night.

It is not suggested that they are being accused of sexual assault, and no-one has been arrested or charged in relation to the alleged incident.

Sympathies across the footy space remain, first and foremost, with the alleged victim, including everyone spoken to for this story.

While finding it difficult to talk about anyone outside of the woman at the centre of this story, AFLW pioneer Chyloe Kurdas told ABC Sport it had been a "horrendous" week for many women in the footy space.

Sydney started its season on a high after a round one victory against Adelaide. (Getty: Mark Brake)

"As women, we live with the fear of sexual assault every day, and so this is not just something that only the Swans AFLW team will be feeling. There will be a fair bit of anger across the whole AFLW system," Kurdas said.

Diversity and inclusion leader Rana Hussain, who has worked across multiple sports including within AFL clubs, said sexual violence was not an abstract issue for women, as many were feeling this story deeply.

In Australia, one in five women have experienced sexual violence over the age of 15, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, and Hussain said: "Even for those who haven't, most women understand its prevalence and have spent their lives learning to navigate and mitigate that risk.

"So these players are likely carrying this both as employees of the Sydney Swans and as women. And now they have to pull on the jumper, represent their club and potentially answer questions about something they had absolutely nothing to do with," Hussain said.

"We need to be really careful that the women of the Sydney Swans aren't asked to carry the cultural and emotional labour of this moment.

"Too often when these issues arise, women are leaned on to explain why it matters, what respectful culture should look like and what needs to change.

"They can love their club and represent it proudly while still asking difficult questions of their leaders about what the club's values actually mean when they are tested. Standing the players down is an important first step, but for the people inside that organisation, the work doesn't end there."

Sydney Swans will be put under an unwanted spotlight this weekend. (Getty: Mark Brake)

The ABC has spoken to sources in and around the AFLW program, who are not able to speak on the record, but conveyed their deep hurt.

One source close to the women's program said there were strong feelings of hurt, anger and humiliation following the actions of the men's players.

The double-header between the programs is the first in the club's history, with the women running out on the SCG for the first time for premiership points on Sunday before the men's game.

While the club will continue to build enthusiasm for the AFLW game against Essendon, the Swans players will have an undesired added layer of attention in what was originally a celebration.

Swans women's players and coaches have yet to comment publicly on the matter. However, that will likely change when they are obliged to do media post-game on Sunday.

Star player Chloe Molloy has already been questioned by media on her way into Swans HQ this week.

"The women, through no fault of their own, there'll be a spotlight put on them because of poor behaviour from men," Kurdas said.

Swans say players 'in serious breach' The Sydney Swans say the players allegedly linked to an incident at a Melbourne hotel "are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

"We don't know what allegedly has happened. But running out there, flying Sydney Swans' flag and playing your role for the club, when you don't know if the boys that play would have your back and play their role for you?"

At a press conference on Wednesday, Sydney CEO Matthew Pavlich said his club's women's team was "deeply disappointed" in the five male players suspended for breaches of club standards and that the club was "supporting them as best they can".

Earlier this week, former AFLW All Australian and now commentator for Seven and Triple M Kate McCarthy questioned how much the AFL space was doing to engage truly and include women and girls in footy spaces safely.

The post was praised by current AFLW players, including GWS' Tilly Lucas-Rodd, while Lions star Jade Ellenger commented: "This is what using a platform for change looks like, so well said."

In a lengthy post, McCarthy wrote in part: "The AFL says it wants women and girls to feel that football belongs to them. That has to mean more than having an AFLW competition or getting women through the gates.

"It means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated, and how our industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise."

World.title: De Minaur suffers US Open seeding blow after Cincinatti boilover
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has missed out on a top-four US Open seeding after crashing out in the fourth round of the Cincinnati Masters.

De Minaur had the chance to climb into the world's top five with a deep run at the final Masters 1000 event before the season's last grand slam in New York.

But the Australian number one delivered a flat performance to fall 6-3, 6-4 to rising Frenchman Arthur Fils in just 82 minutes on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

De Minaur dropped serve once in each set and was unable to break the 21st seed at all.

The world number eight's exit means de Minaur is certain to be seeded in the top eight at Flushing Meadows, still ensuring the Australian does not run into a higher-ranked player until at least the quarterfinals.

But with Carlos Alcaraz still injured, de Minaur could have snatched a US Open top-four seeding and been guaranteed to avoid heavyweights such as Jannik Sinner and Alexander Zverev until at least the semifinals.

Australian qualifier Chris O'Connell plays his fourth-round match in Cincinnati later on Thursday against American sixth seed Taylor Fritz.

AAP

World.title: 'Have they brought value?': McIlroy fires shot at returning LIV Golf stars
World.content:
Masters champion Rory McIlroy believes it could be a "tough road back" for LIV Golf players who may be eyeing a return to the PGA Tour and questioned what value they would even offer the US-based circuit.

McIlroy, speaking to reporters ahead of this week's BMW Championship, needed a brief moment to reflect before answering a question on whether the possibility of players returning from LIV Golf brings value to the PGA Tour.

"I mean, I would argue, have they brought value to LIV? You know?" McIlroy said at Bellerive Country Club in St Louis, Missouri.

"I think the PGA Tour's in a really good spot."

Australia's Cameron Smith is among the LIV Golf cohort that is yet to return to the PGA Tour. (Getty Images: Jamie Squire)

LIV Golf is wrapping up its 2026 season this week near Indianapolis and said earlier this month that it had secured a lead investor that will provide a funding boost as it prepares for a future without backing from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

It remains unclear, however, whether major champions ⁠Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm, two of LIV Golf's biggest draws, will stay on with the rebel circuit beyond this season or seek a return to the PGA Tour.

Brooks Koepka took advantage of a limited-time Returning Member Program in early 2026 to rejoin the PGA Tour after leaving LIV Golf last December.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Koepka's return came at a cost, with the five-time major winner facing a five-year forfeiture of potential equity in the PGA Tour's Player Equity Program, representing an estimated $50–85 million loss depending on his performance and tour growth.

DeChambeau, Rahm and former British Open champion Cameron Smith were also eligible to return under the same Returning Member Program that closed on February 2 after a three-week application window.

McIlroy said he was pretty certain that any additional returning players would not be welcomed back straight away.

"If they were offered this returning member program back in February, the one that Brooks took, then, yeah, maybe. But that has sort of come and gone," he said.

"And I think it was said at the time that the deal that they might get going forward, if they do decide to come back, isn't going to be as good as the one that Brooks got. So, yeah, I would say it's going to be a tough, tough road back."

Reuters

World.title: Socceroos star Circati seals $33m transfer move to Portuguese giants
World.content:
Young Socceroo Alessandro Circati has become the latest Australian international to be snapped up in a money-spinning European transfer, as he hails his move from Parma to Benfica as a "privilege".

Following Lucas Herrington's move from the MLS to become Australia's only Premier League player at Hull City, and Nestory Irankunda joining Benfica's great rivals Sporting from Watford, Circati has been signed by the Portuguese giants for a reported 20 million euros ($33 million).

With Nishan Velupillay's move from Melbourne Victory to third-tier German club FC Ingolstadt 04 also completed on Wednesday, World Cup Socceroos are clearly the flavour of the month, with other reports linking top clubs with Norwich striker Mohamed Toure.

Circati's move from the Italian top-flight Serie A to Portugal's Primeira Liga has been in the pipeline for a while, with the 22-year-old having signed a five-year contract through to 2031 with the Lisbon-based double European champions.

"To all the Benfiquistas, yeah, I can't wait to play in front of you all, and win as many titles as we can. It's a huge honour. It's a privilege. I'm over the moon, couldn't be happier," Circati said in a message to the fans on the club's website.

"I think it's a reward for many years of hard work. I'm so happy to be here, and I can't wait to play for Benfica."

The Italian-born Circati will play at the world-famous Estadio da Luz — the Stadium of Light — and sounded just a little awe-struck as he added: "I can't wait. I've just had a look at it now. It's amazing, and I'm very, very excited to play."

Socceroos forward Nishan Velupillay (right) is also moving to a new club, joining Germany's FC Ingolstadt 04. (Reuters: Albert Gea)

Asked about adapting quickly to his move, he added: "I think I'm very adaptable. I think you can play me in either role of the centre-back, in a back-four or a back-three.

"I'm sure it's going to take a bit of time to adapt, but I'll try and make it as fast as possible with the help of my teammates and staff. But I'm sure I'll fit in just fine."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The lad who came through the ranks at Perth Glory and, after completing a trial with Parma in 2021, returned to his Italian roots to join them, has made swift and impressive progress in Serie A, last year being a stand-out for the northern club as they finished 12th.

Circati also played in all four of the Socceroos' World Cup matches, with 17 international appearances now under his belt and one goal to his name.

Parma paid tribute to his time at the club in a statement, saying: "Alessandro made a total of 96 appearances for Parma, including 37 in Serie A, scoring two goals and playing a key role not only in the club's 2023/24 Serie B title triumph but also in securing survival over the following two seasons.

"President Kyle J. Krause, CEO Federico Cherubini and the entire Parma Calcio family would like to sincerely thank Alessandro and wish him every success in the next chapter of his career."

AAP

World.title: FIFA vice-president withdraws support for Infantino after 'final straw'
World.content:
More national football federations and FIFA officials have withdrawn their support for the football body's president, Gianni Infantino, after the exit of chief operating officer Kevin Lamour, which one FIFA vice-president described as the "final straw".

FIFA said on Tuesday (AEST) that Lamour had left the organisation. It came weeks after he publicly criticised Mr Infantino's plan to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other tournaments.

His exit prompted Hungary's Sandor Csanyi — one of eight FIFA vice-presidents and a member of the FIFA Council — to withdraw his support for the embattled Mr Infantino, who is under pressure from three confederations to resign.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"The final straw was the unexpected dismissal of Kevin Lamour," Mr Csanyi wrote in a letter to Infantino, seen by Reuters.

"Kevin performed his duties to a high professional and ethical standard and, as a highly competent executive, made a significant contribution to the transparent operation of the organisation.

"The fact that his dismissal was prompted by his criticism of the above-mentioned initiative — an initiative that you yourself ultimately acknowledged to have been misguided — points to serious shortcomings in professional judgement, ethical standards and leadership."

FIFA did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr Lamour had said staff had been "deceived" over the plan, which he described as the project of one person.

Other FIFA vice-presidents who have attacked Mr Infantino's conduct are UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin, AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al-Khalifa, and CONCACAF president Vittorio Montagliani.

'Extremely worrying'

Dejan Savicevic has labelled recent developments at FIFA under Infantino's tenure "extremely worrying". (Getty Images: Gualter Fatia)

Montenegro's Dejan Savicevic, a FIFA Council member since 2017 and president of the country's football association, said they had also withdrawn their earlier letter of support for Mr Infantino's candidacy.

Mr Infantino is up for re-election in March and is seeking a fourth term until 2031.

Mr Savicevic wrote a letter to FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström outlining his concerns.

"The recent developments within FIFA are extremely worrying and have shown a serious lack of communication and transparency not only to the member associations … but also to the internal members, FIFA Council included, and structures which should hold the foundations of FIFA," he wrote.

"The proposals put forward exposed concerning vulnerabilities regarding governance, not only at the political level but also within the FIFA administration.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The Football Association of Montenegro agrees with the opinion of other European national associations and UEFA and demands a thorough review of the actions of the FIFA leadership," he added.

Israel has also withdrawn its support for Mr Infantino's re-election, according to The Guardian, with the decision being taken unanimously after a meeting of the IFA's board.

Football Association of Wales (FAW) chief executive Noel Mooney told the BBC that Mr Infantino should resign after his doomed proposal to "sell off the crown jewels" to private equity investors.

Earlier this month, Wales became the first national federation to withdraw its support for Mr Infantino formally.

Despite the opposition of the three confederations, African confederation CAF and South America's CONMEBOL are currently on Mr Infantino's side.

CAF president Patrice Motsepe, who is also a FIFA vice-president, warned any attempt to remove him should be decided democratically by FIFA's 211-member associations at next year's elections, rather than through other means.

A CAF spokesperson said Mr Motsepe had nothing further to add after Mr Lamour's exit.

Reuters

World.title: Olympic questions 'off limits' ahead of Rockhampton schools' rowing regatta
World.content:
Rowing Queensland has imposed new media restrictions on athletes, coaches and rowing representatives ahead of an upcoming state schools regatta at the proposed Brisbane 2032 rowing venue.

Next month's Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta will bring more than 800 school-aged rowers from across Queensland to Rockhampton for three days of racing on the Fitzroy River, the controversial venue selected to host rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Olympics and Paralympics.

It will be the first state-level rowing event held at the venue in five years, placing a renewed spotlight on the Fitzroy River's suitability for major competition.

Rockhampton school rowers training on the Fitzroy River. (Supplied: Rockhampton Grammar School)

But in a significant development, the ABC understands local rowing representatives preparing for the championships were told they could not discuss or promote the Olympics in media interviews.

Rowing Queensland has confirmed it introduced a stricter media accreditation process for the event amid heightened media interest and safeguarding concerns around school-aged rowers.

Chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin said she appreciated the increased interest in rowing in Rockhampton given its link to Brisbane 2032, but the schools' regatta should not be viewed as a test or demonstration event for the Olympics.

Tim Mander (far left) and David Crisafulli (centre) meet school rowers on the Fitzroy River, the proposed venue for rowing at the 2032 Brisbane Olympics. (Supplied: Queensland Government)

"At the request of the local rowing club, Rowing Queensland has introduced a media accreditation process for the championship," Ms O'Loughlin said.

" Our priority is to provide an environment where school-aged athletes can train and compete safely, without additional media pressure or disruption. "

She said locals were free to discuss the Olympics and events coming to Rockhampton but stressed the upcoming regatta was a school event being held on infrastructure appropriate for school sport.

The Queensland government has repeatedly defended the Fitzroy River as a suitable venue for the 2032 Games, dismissing concerns about the natural river course, flooding, crocodiles, infrastructure and racing conditions.

Jarrod Bleijie says the rowing will happen on the Fitzroy River for the 2032 Games. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Speaking in Toowoomba on Thursday morning, Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said he was disappointed there were restrictions on "people talking positively about rowing on the mighty Fitzroy River".

"People should be able to talk openly about the benefits of regional Queensland, the benefits of rowing on the mighty Fitzroy River and how great it's going to be in 2032," he said.

" Secondly, I'd say this: I might even go now. I might go to the state championships because I'd love to see some of these organisations try and gag me from speaking to the media, particularly about how great rowing at the 2032 Games is going to be on the mighty Fitzroy River. "

Members of the CQ32 Rowing Legacy Advisory Committee, which is championing the Fitzroy River as the venue for rowing and canoeing at the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

The Olympic proposal

The proposal to hold Olympic rowing on the Fitzroy River was first championed by a Central Queensland advocacy group which included Queensland senator and National Party leader Matt Canavan.

"The Rockhampton rowing course is at the centre of everything with an airport, highway and a CBD within minutes," Senator Canavan said at the time.

"It just all stacks up. I think the Games should deliver for all of Queensland."

Mining magnate Gina Rinehart also wrote to Queensland's deputy premier advocating for Olympic rowing and canoeing to be held in Rockhampton before the venue was selected.

Australian rowers have previously used the Fitzroy River as a training venue before the Olympics. (ABC Capricornia: Alice Roberts)

Rowing Queensland supports the Queensland government in hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the state but says the proposed Rockhampton venue remains subject to the technical and venue planning processes associated with hosting an Olympic event.

Ms O'Loughlin said the existing Rockhampton course and infrastructure were appropriate for a school-level competition but were not representative of what would be required for a national, international or Olympic rowing event.

"The rowing community awaits the release of information on the Olympic venue location and infrastructure, which has yet to be published by the Queensland government," she said.

A crocodile warning sign at the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Tobias Jurss-Lewis)

Scrutiny of venue

Concerns have nevertheless been raised by rowing bodies and elite Australian rowers about fairness, tidal currents and the suitability of a natural river course, including issues around flooding and crocodile management, with some advocating for dedicated facilities in south-east Queensland or interstate.

Rowing Australia said the technical assessment of the Rockhampton venue was a matter for the relevant authorities, including World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee.

It said it would continue to support key stakeholders involved in planning for Brisbane 2032.

An electronic billboard in Rockhampton has been up for several months, alternating between designs promoting the Olympics for central Queensland. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

Asked where Rowing Queensland believed Olympic rowing should be held, Ms O'Loughlin said the organisation was not involved in the venue-selection process.

"Rowing Queensland's position is that Olympic rowing should be held in Queensland at a venue that meets the technical requirements for Olympic competition and receives the necessary approval through the Olympic venue-assessment process," she said.

"Rowing Queensland awaits the outcomes of the relevant technical review, including the assessment by World Rowing."

Australian rowers Jess Morrison and Annabelle McIntyre competing at the 2024 Paris Olympics. (AAP via Photosport: Iain McGregor)

'Games for Queensland'

In March, the state's Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority progressed its feasibility assessment for the Rockhampton Flatwater Facility to evaluate two preferred layouts, moving the high-stakes 2032 Games venue into its next detailed planning phase.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the latest progress ensured the Rockhampton community and competitors could have confidence in the Fitzroy.

Hundreds of athletes will compete in state championship events from year 9 through to year 12 next month. (Supplied: Rockhampton Grammar School)

"The Crisafulli government promised a Games and generational legacy for all Queenslanders, including rowing and canoeing in Rocky," Mr Bleijie said.

"We're working well with the rowing and canoeing international federations, as well as the IOC and our Games delivery partners to deliver an incredible venue and competition in 2032, and a long-lasting legacy for Rockhampton."

The Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta will be held on the Fitzroy River from September 19 to 21, marking the pinnacle event and conclusion of the 2026 Queensland school rowing season.

World.title: Longmire reveals 'deep sadness' over Swans' links to police probe
World.content:
Sydney's last premiership coach says there is a deep sense of sadness at five banned Swans players being linked to allegations of sexual assault.

John Longmire, the Swans' longest-serving coach, says the suspensions of five players are "flattening" for all involved.

Swans Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon are linked to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel on Monday morning.

'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident Five Sydney Swans players stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards issue an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad detectives are expected to soon arrive in Sydney to further their investigations.

The players are yet to be formally interviewed or charged, and it is not suggested that any of them are being accused of sexual assault.

The bans instead related to the players' decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women to their hotel, for which they have apologised.

Longmire, who is currently the club's executive director of club performance, said the on-field ramifications of banning the players were not a priority for the Swans hierarchy.

"It was just incredible deep sadness … and that is probably where we're still sitting," he told Fox Footy on Wednesday night.

Longmire was the coach when Sydney won its most recent AFL premiership in 2012. (AAP: Joe Castro)

"Football aspirations weren't part of the discussions, they were very much in the background.

"At the forefront were other people issues — as they should have been.

"The people issues are the things that really led the discussions over the last few days … the premiership discussions were at the very back-end of anything that was talked about."

The second-placed Swans, with one home-and-away game remaining, are assured of hosting two finals as they seek to win the club's first premiership since under Longmire in 2012.

"It's flattening for a lot of people," he said.

John Longmire with Isaac Heeney after the 2024 preliminary final. (Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

"It's a challenge for everybody to be able to get through and be able to put one foot in front of the other and get things right.

"We feel for everybody."

Longmire was Sydney's head coach from 2011 to 2024 after being an assistant from 2002.

"The culture of the footy club has taken a big hit, and it will take time for everyone to rebuild the trust in the football club," he said.

"You go from shock and disappointment, maybe a bit of anger in that. You get a bit of those emotions.

"And you also care about people, try and get that balance right, and it's very tricky."

The five players on Wednesday evening apologised in a joint statement issued by the Swans.

"We are deeply sorry to everyone involved," they said. "We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club.

"We accept the club sanction and apologise for the impact this has had on those involved."

Meanwhile, Readings Books and Gleebooks have confirmed they have removed Heeney's children's book series, Little Isaac Footy Fever, for purchase, after Allen & Unwin also removed promotions for the books from their Instagram grid.

Booktopia said they will continue to stock the book but will assess the situation.

"We're working closely with the publisher regarding their plans and will continue to assess the situation," a statement provided to the ABC said.

"Our mandate is to provide a service and selection of books in the best interest of our customers. We appreciate the sensitivity and will carefully consider any decision, together with the publisher, in due course."

ABC/AAP

Tech.title: Does giving a camera wings dodge the FCC’s drone ban?
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DJI ban: how the world’s biggest dronemaker is getting shoved out of the US

HoverAir drones always have intriguing gimmicks. This one folds flat to fit in your pocket. This one can land on water. Another can charge inside its carrying case. But the brand’s latest trick might be its riskiest: it’s attempting to sneak a drone past the FCC.

In December 2025, the US government banned future foreign drones from reaching our shores, and HoverAir’s floating Aqua drone was one of the first casualties. But this time, brand owner Zero Zero Robotics might have found a loophole: its latest $750 Versa drone isn’t a drone, it claims, but rather a DJI Pocket-style mini steadycam with optional snap-on propellers that let it fly.

“The Flight Kit is an accessory that extends VERSA’s capabilities. Therefore, HOVERAir is in full compliance with the applicable regulatory requirements for the full product configuration offered to US customers,” global marketing director Anita Facundo tells The Verge.

As far as HoverAir is publicly concerned, the gambit has already worked. The FCC already approved the new HoverAir Versa on August 9th, public records show, and the company just launched it on Indiegogo this week while telling customers it’s good to go.

But the reality is more complicated. I’ve read through the full text of the FCC’s orders, and there’s reason to believe the loophole is real. But there’s also reason to believe the FCC was fooled and could easily reject this drone.

Zero Zero got its authorization grant for the Versa on August 9th. Images: FCC

When the FCC’s foreign drone ban came down in December, it blocked the FCC from automatically approving the radios of any foreign-made drone — each company now has to convince the FCC that its drone is either made in the United States, or doesn’t pose a threat to national security. (Or, lie on the paperwork.)

But while the ban automatically creates friction for every kind of drone, it doesn’t affect every dronemaker’s cameras — only those from DJI and Autel Robotics, because those were the two specifically named in the 2025 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

HoverAir effectively says “we’re not on the Covered List…for cameras.” Image: FCC

When HoverAir submitted its paperwork to the FCC, it only did so for the camera portion of its drone. It told the FCC’s agent, truthfully, that HoverAir has not been banned from getting cameras certified in the US. The FCC’s agent, one of the private companies known as Telecommunications Certification Bodies (TCB), signed off on that basis.

What about the propeller wings that turn it into a drone? Well, the FCC only certifies gadgets that have a wireless radio inside — the propellers almost certainly don’t, since they physically connect to the camera using copper contacts. HoverAir might not have to submit them to the FCC at all.

That’s the loophole, but it might not be so simple. See, the FCC’s foreign drone ban isn’t just on “drones” but also “UAS critical components,” and the camera clearly contains many of the critical components that make HoverAir’s drone fly. The FCC has explicitly said that cameras are one of those critical components. And because HoverAir’s camera has radios, it is under the FCC’s jurisdiction.

Like usual, the FCC outsourced its original decision to certify the HoverAir Versa to a private company, but it’s likely to take a second look itself now that HoverAir is trying this loophole. And if it decides that the Versa is a “UAS critical component,” it has a little-known tool to quickly reverse the decision.

The FCC can easily nix a certification within 30 days, and we’re not outside that period for HoverAir yet.

To be fair to HoverAir, it did begin offering refunds when it became clear the Aqua would not ship in the US. It’s also selling the Versa camera by itself, though only 12 Indiegogo backers seem to be opting for that as I type these words.

I badly want to try this flying camera. It looks fun! But here in the US, I wouldn’t personally put money towards a Versa till I know the FCC’s OK with it.

With new drones, routers, robots, and Roombas all at the FCC’s whims, we sure do live in interesting times.

Tech.title: Nielsen is leaning more on wearables to hear what people are watching
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

In order to beef up its ability to accurately measure viewership data in the streaming era, Nielsen is moving forward with a plan to use more information gathered from its partners’ wearable devices.

Today, Nielsen announced “a number of key enhancements” that are being added to its data capturing process ahead of the upcoming fall TV season. As of August 31st, Nielsen’s co-viewing data will now include information obtained from smart-watch like gadgets that Neilsen’s research panelists wear in their homes. The Portable People Meter (PPM) Wearables — which Nielsen first began deploying nationally in 2016 to bolster its audio, local TV, and national audience measurements — are meant to be worn on the wrist while listening for audio from TV scenes, series, and films. The company says that users wearing the devices won’t need to go through the typical Nielsen log in process, and it believes that incorporating this technology into its processes will give it a better idea “of how many people are watching a given program.”

Building on its decision from earlier this year to adopt the Advertising Research Foundation’s (ARF) Device and Account Sharing (DASH) data into its methodology, Nielsen will use new DASH estimates that are based on more recent survey data. The company will also use data from two additional surveys in order to better estimate how many Spanish-speaking households are in its pool of panel participants. Nielsen is also updating the machine learning tool it uses to process information from data providers to assess the demographic makeup of individual households, which means. The firm noted that this last update should help “ensure the data is more representative and does not artificially skew toward older residents.”

Each of these new features makes it sound like Nielsen is taking even more stops to maintain its position as the industry standard for ratings capture at the time when people’s viewing habits have become much more fractured. The company also has to contend with the way the rise of streaming makes it difficult to accurately assess what people are watching. Being asked to keep Nielsen’s proprietary devices in their homes is nothing new for the company’s panel participants, but the push to wear listening wearables could strike some as a bit intrusive. But if this all really does lead to Nielsen capturing more reliable information, other firms might follow its example.

Tech.title: Google Gemini is getting a dedicated student hub
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

As we’re gearing up for back-to-school season, Google is rolling out a new dedicated student hub in Gemini. It’s a one-stop repository for collecting research in a study notebook, creating flashcards, taking practice quizzes, and more. Google is also enhancing its study notebooks with support for graphs and images. It can even add test dates and deadlines to your Google Calendar based on your syllabus.

Google is also adding Deep Research to Gemini Live. You can ask Gemini to generate complicated research reports and talk through the results. If it’s taking a while, you can close the chat and lock your phone screen, and Gemini will let you know when your report is ready. In the coming weeks, it will also start rolling out a new feature for Lens in the Google mobile app that lets you take a photo of your study or worksheet and get explanations, help with complicated concepts, or even coaching if you’ve made a mistake.

Eligible students in the US can score one year of Google AI Pro for free, which includes 5TB of storage, Google Health Premium, higher usage limits on Gemini, and access to Gemini across Google apps. Students outside the US will have to make do with the slightly less comprehensive Google AI Plus sub, which comes with 400GB of storage and lower Gemini usage limits.

Tech.title: Watch Valve set up the Steam Frame in its own leaked videos
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Valve just leaked several new videos showing the Steam Frame’s unboxing, setup process, and various accessories. The videos apparently appeared on the ARM Steam client following an update, but they were “quickly pulled after that,” according to the Steam Hardware Updates account on X.

The Steam Frame is Valve’s virtual-reality headset that can stream games from a PC or play them locally. Valve first took the wraps off the headset last year, and it offers LCD screens with 2160 x 2160 resolution per eye, a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip, and an up to 110-degree field of view. But these leaked videos offer a closer look at what it might be like to unbox and set up the new device.

As shown in one of the videos, Valve shows how you can use the Steam Frame’s “pivot arms” to adjust the position of the headset, as well as how to insert a spacer beneath the face gasket if you wear glasses. Another video details how you can plug the wireless dongle into your PC or Steam Machine to stream games.

Though Valve previously said that it plans to release the Steam Frame this summer, it hasn’t yet shared an exact launch date. Still, that timeframe, these setup videos, and a recent 13-ton shipment of VR headsets could all indicate that a launch is right around the corner.

Tech.title: The wearable future is stuck in weird, experimental, existential limbo
Tech.content:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

For the past week, I’ve been testing the Google Pixel Watch 5. In many ways, it’s a typical, modern smartwatch. In others, it feels like one part of a wearable future that’s increasingly in flux. Everyone I’ve spoken to in wearable tech has roughly the same goal — soon, your tracker of choice will feature a helpful AI coach, “check engine” alerts that preventively flag hard-to-detect health conditions, and personalized health recommendations based on your lived experiences and needs.

That’s certainly what’s being pitched. But so far, it seems like most companies don’t know how exactly we’re going to get there.

AI coaches? Even the best ones are too chatty, fixate on one random detail you shared during setup, and require a ton of hand-holding. “Check engine” alerts can be useful and have been documented as saving lives. They can also spark health anxiety and the regulatory quagmire can be expensive to navigate. Personalized health holds great promise, but requires so much of your private data while also being subject to AI’s myriad shortcomings. Even now, most people think of wearable devices as fancy step trackers.

“Historically, wearables have been very focused on hardcore health enthusiasts,” Rishi Chandra, Google’s vice president of health and home, tells me at a roundtable of tech reporters in New York ahead of Made by Google. Usually, tech companies like to keep mum on future ideas and plans. But recently, Google seems eager to lay out its particular vision.

“There’s a huge market of people who are not thinking about their health every day. Today, wearable penetration is about 30 percent — 70 percent of the population has no notion of wearables,” Chandra adds.

Waraich says Google views “glanceble” interactions as lasting roughly seven seconds.

In other words, wearable tech is still in its early days with a lot of untapped potential. The smartwatch is not the end-all, be-all. The fact that wearables can also capture a vast array of personal data compounds that. That’s one reason why, during last year’s Made by Google event, Chandra and Sandeep Waraich, Google’s senior director of wearables, told me that the future of AI gadgets won’t just be a single device. It’ll be an entire ecosystem of diverse accessories.

Since that chat, I’ve already seen several signs supporting Google’s multi-wearable ecosystem thesis. Multiple companies have pivoted to AI glasses (or as Google calls it, “intelligent eyewear”). But we’ve also seen other wearable form factors start gaining steam. See: the horde of screenless Whoop dupes and smart rings. In the AI sphere, some wearable makers are eschewing the health tracking aspect altogether. Some smart jewelry startups like Vocci, Taya, and Sandbar envision rings and pendants as a way to record and transcribe your thoughts using AI.

These are not proven ideas. That there are so many different approaches is a pretty big indication that the entire industry is in the process of throwing wearable spaghetti at a wall, desperately hoping that something will stick and be the next smartphone. It’s enough to make a senior wearable reviewer excited — because yay! Weird experimental products — and also mad — because no! Weird experimental products that don’t work as advertised! Still, there’s a nugget of truth in this new search for new wearable form factors and use cases.

“Wearables are a great conduit for presence. And it goes both ways. As AI reaches you in a respectful way, and as you want to interact with it, these interactions will become more frequent, but also quicker and glanceable,” says Waraich, noting that Google views seven seconds as its current benchmark for any one wrist-based interaction. The question now is figuring out the ideal surface for each specific technological task. For example: What device should you use to check your calendar? Your phone, tablet, or laptop? Or, with the addition of the Proactive Assistance feature on the Pixel Watch 5, should it be your smartwatch?

A Google or Fitbit smart ring is not on the table right now. Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

According to Chandra and Waraich, Google has had deep internal discussions about the pros and cons of various wearable form factors. Smart rings, for instance, are something that Google consistently gets asked about but won’t be pursuing in the short term.

“To be clear, we’re not closing the door on [smart rings],” Chandra says. “But our belief right now is that there’s so much headroom on a wrist-worn wearable … I think the Fitbit Air is going to have far bigger expansion opportunities given how simple and easy it is for everyone to use it.”

Okay, so Google just introduced the minimalist Fitbit Air and for now is passing on smart rings. Perhaps then the next step is an “Ultra” Pixel Watch as Samsung and Apple have done. Not so. When I ask, Waraich explains the current Pixel Watch is where Google sees its premium offerings. Chandra adds that the company is wary of spreading itself too thin.

Google certainly has a hypothesis of what wearable tech ought to be. It’s placing its bets through product launches and software updates, watching carefully to see how we — the wearable lab rats — react to specific ideas. The experiment continues.

Another wearable debate: whether it makes sense to add in microphones just because you can. For example, putting mics in something like the Fitbit Air so that it can also double as your AI memory — something akin to Amazon’s Bee device.

“At this point, it’s not a technology issue. It’s a user-sentiment, privacy issue. If you [add] a mic, it’s not just that it’s learning from you. It’s learning from the environment. So I think we’re being cautious about how to push that in the right way,” Chandra says, noting it’d have been easy for Google to stuff microphones into the Fitbit Air but the actual problem is whether doing so would add any customer value. “I don’t know yet if we have, as a tech industry, have figured out the right balancing act there.”

Having tested several AI wearables, my answer is a resounding hell no. As I’ve written on the site, this type of AI wearable tech often makes me feel like a spy. Similarly, I’ll simply point to the defunct Amazon Halo trackers, which not only tracked your emotions based on the tone of your voice but also created highly cursed, self-esteem-obliterating 3D models of your body to estimate fat percentages. Just because AI wearables can track new things doesn’t mean they should.

The Fitbit Air and other wrist-worn wearables, Google says, have more runway than other form factors. Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

This problem also plagues smart glasses, as seen with the recent privacy backlash toward Meta’s “pervert glasses.” Some of that is Meta’s penchant for sticking its foot in it. Some of that, Google argues, is perhaps a matter of time and place. Perhaps, Chandra notes, people are more amenable to ambient computing — where your devices are always listening — inside the home instead of outside of it.

Even so, Google is committed to experimenting. What if, Waraich posited, the camera in smart glasses simply acted as a sensor without recording? As in, the glasses see what you see and can answer questions about your environment, but nothing gets recorded for posterity. In theory, this might mean the ability to automatically log your food without ever having to take a picture. A blind person might be able to ask an AI questions about their surroundings, and passersby wouldn’t have to worry that a photo of them exists in someone else’s camera roll.

To that, I say: Love the concept, good luck communicating how that’s different to the masses.

This is part of the existential problem facing my beat. How can any AI wearable be versatile enough to account for every individual’s privacy preferences and health journey? It’s easy enough to differentiate the hardware. Casual users? You get a Fitbit Air or Oura Ring. Tech nerds tired of their phones? Depending on your phone, I’ll point you to a Pixel Watch or Apple Watch. Oh, you’re entering an Ironman? I already know you’re wondering which flavor of Garmin or Coros suits you best.

But the software experience is a whole ’nother beast. Right now you can pick from multiple wearable form factors, but they all pretty much give you the same cluttered app and whap you over the head with data fatigue. That’s hardly a recipe for personalized health. I’ve shared over the course of several Optimizers that my current health journey relates to fixing my borked metabolism. That requires one set of advice. A cancer patient would need something wholly different. So would a hypochondriac or a young college athlete. Maybe you like a drill-sergeant-type coach. Or, if you’re like me, that type of tough love would make you want to throw up your hands. It’s already hard enough for people to learn how to be wise and judicious about their health, to accept limits and practice compassion without veering into overindulgence. How the hell can any one LLM achieve that wisdom? How can we expect one cluttered, unified software experience to meet the needs of an infinite number of individual needs?

AI is often seen as the key to data context and personalized health. It’s defintely a work in progress. Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

I asked both Chandra and Waraich this. Both were optimistic that AI will one day get there, but it isn’t there currently. They acknowledged that this is a yearslong journey that will require lots and lots of work. That there are a lot of societal and cultural questions that’ll have to be debated internally and externally. After a decade, my wearable bullshit radar is strong, and since Wear OS 3, Google has genuinely welcomed a good wearable grilling whenever I (or other reporters) have offered frank feedback. I can’t say the same for every gadgetmaker on my beat.

I also can’t tell whether Google’s making all the right wearable bets with the Pixel Watch 5, Fitbit Air, or its AI coach. Maybe it’s a whiff to pass on smart rings. I still think I need to see more proof that an AI hardware ecosystem of diverse accessories is the ultimate move. I’ll give Google credit for being so candid about the multiple layers of privacy, culture, design, and tech logistics that go into the current era of wearable gadgets. That said, whenever I zoom out, I can’t help but feel like I’m caught in the proverbial hamster wheel. Testing each new smartwatch, smart ring, or smart glasses, I keep running toward this vaguely defined, AI-powered wearable future. I just don’t feel any closer to reaching it.

Tech.title: OpenAI hit the brakes. Now what?
Tech.content:
With a looming IPO, intense competition from Anthropic, and Chinese and open-weight rivals nipping at its heels, OpenAI has plenty of reasons to move fast. Instead, it hit the brakes.

On Tuesday, the company said it had slowed the pace of some AI development while it tightened security and safeguards. That included a two-week pause in reinforcement learning training on its “latest models intended for deployment,” and an ongoing delay to its “largest planned frontier RL run.”

The decision is a very public test of an idea AI safety advocates have pushed for for years: that companies should be willing to bow out of the AI race and slow things down when their safeguards fail to keep up with what they are building. But as the race around them continues, will slowing down accomplish anything?

“For the pause to be sustainable, it has to be made industry-wide.”

For all the talk of slowing down, OpenAI isn’t exactly standing still. The company said it is “pacing” development, a fuzzy and imprecise term that has nevertheless become part of the industry’s lexicon in recent months. In practice, the slowdown is narrowly scoped. OpenAI’s announcement says the pause only covers models meant for deployment while it beefs up security and monitoring before it runs the kind of tests where models may be capable of getting out and hacking real targets. It doesn’t necessarily mean there will be a significant slowdown of the company’s broader development.

From the outside, it’s hard to tell how sincere OpenAI is about stopping solely for the sake of safety, particularly when the company and senior staff have been so vocal about it. But the company’s commitment to safety has been called into question in recent months following a series of high-profile safety team departures and the disbanding of its preparedness team. OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

There are good reasons to take OpenAI’s slowdown seriously. Experts who spoke to The Verge pointed to the costs of slowing down at a time of intense competition. Every delay gives rivals more time to catch up or extend their lead. “Due to the intensity of the AI race, everyone has an incentive to work at breakneck speed,” said Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and cofounder of Apollo Research, an AI safety research organization. “Voluntarily slowing down worsens your positioning in the race, so it’s not something that a lab would do lightly.”

The decision also broadly fits with OpenAI’s own published safety doctrine, its Preparedness Framework, as well as the safety frameworks of other AI companies, said Alan Chan, a research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI. “The basic principle is: Continue with development and/or deployment only when we have the mitigations that enable doing so with acceptable risk,” Chan said. As part of the new safety measures, OpenAI said it plans to review and “evolve” the framework — much of which dates back to 2023, when it was first published — to account for advances in its models.

There are also good reasons to believe the new safeguards will actually make OpenAI’s systems safer, at least in the short term, though experts cautioned that this is difficult to assess without more information. “These are good steps that, implemented well, are probably enough to prevent the current generation of agents from causing harm,” Adam Gleave, cofounder and CEO of AI safety organization FAR.AI, told The Verge. “The key question is how OpenAI will keep pace as capabilities increase.”

Gleave’s question points to a broader problem: If technical safeguards falter again, what then? Nothing required OpenAI to stop and take stock this time, which is what made its willingness to do so meaningful. But it also means there is nothing guaranteeing OpenAI — or any other AI company — will make the same choice next time.

“Pacing buys time, not safety… An effective pacing strategy cannot be improvised during a crisis.”

Relying on companies to make that call themselves is a precarious form of governance, particularly in an industry where, as Hobbhahn noted, there is every incentive to keep going. Nick Moës, executive director of nonprofit AI safety and governance organization The Future Society, described self-policing as the structural problem at the heart of the current approach to AI safety. He argued it should be possible for governments to decide whether OpenAI or any other company should pause development of a technology deemed unsafe. “This is how most industries operate,” he said, pointing to drugs, construction, aircraft, and even restaurants as sectors with stronger regulatory oversight than AI.

Voluntary measures also risk the industry converging on the lowest common denominator. If slowing down imposes a cost, companies have an incentive to adopt only the measures their rivals are also willing to accept. That pressure becomes particularly acute as the race tightens. If OpenAI repeatedly slows down development while its competitors do not, it “will simply be replaced by Anthropic,” Moës argued. “For the pause to be sustainable, it has to be made industry-wide.”

Sustainable safety needs something stronger than voluntary action. Moës said government oversight could fill that void, as it does in other industries. Independent verification could play a part too. Chan said making sure companies actually implement safety measures will be especially important as technical mitigations like monitoring AIs becomes more expensive. Hobbhahn concurred: “It’s always hard to tell from the outside if a lab is sincere about pausing or safety more broadly, so having more evidence and an independent party to validate the claim is super important.”

Even a perfectly transparent pause is only useful if something actually happens during it. “Pacing buys time, not safety,” said Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy. The point is to create breathing room for companies and governments to understand risks and respond appropriately. This would mean deciding what would trigger a slowdown — as well as what happens during one and conditions needed to end one — ahead of time. “An effective pacing strategy cannot be improvised during a crisis,” she said.

It’s possible OpenAI’s slowdown will set a precedent for the industry. Many of the experts The Verge spoke to hoped other companies would follow its lead, whether voluntary or because stronger rules eventually compel them to. But in an industry still largely policed by itself, there is little stopping its competitors — or OpenAI itself — from racing straight past that precedent next time safety and speed conflict.

Tech.title: GTA VI keeps leaking ahead of its gameplay premiere
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Clips of what appears to be Grand Theft Auto VI have hit the internet, possibly spoiling aspects of the game ahead of Rockstar Games’ deep dive debuting on Netflix next week and its long-awaited launch in November.

I’ve seen three clips seemingly showing off the game, though two have been pulled from the site I saw them on “due to a copyright claim.” The first clip (now removed) was a quiet scene that mostly focused on Jason Duval, one the game’s two protagonists, shooting a basketball into a hoop. Another clip (also removed) featured more of the crime-focused gameplay you’d expect from GTA, including Duval hitting a person with a wrench, and also showed the return of a six-star Wanted system.

A third clip, which is live as I write this, shows Duval driving at night, punching some people, using a taser, and stealing a truck. The clip then jumps to what looks like a cutscene from a different part of the game in the daytime.

The videos were watermarked by a person or group identifying themselves as “CyberLeek.” The third clip has a call for viewers to buy a CyberLeek cryptocurrency, a QR code, links to some sketchy-looking CyberLeek URLs, and a statement that says “NO PHYSICAL DISCS? THEN MORE LEEKS!”, which is seemingly a reference to Rockstar’s decision not to launch GTA VI on a physical disc.

This isn’t the first time apparent footage from GTA VI has leaked. In 2022, 90 videos leaked online long before the game’s official reveal more than a year later (a reveal that also leaked, leading Rockstar to publish the game’s first trailer a day early). A teen who played a key role in leaking the 90 videos was sentenced to life in a secure hospital. Rockstar also confirmed earlier this year that it had data compromised in a hack of a third-party provider, but said the incident would have “no impact on our organization or our players.”

Rockstar and owner Take-Two didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. The GTA VI “extended look” premieres on Netflix on August 27th at 3PM ET and will stream on YouTube at 9PM ET. The $79.99 title is scheduled to launch on November 19th, and for the most part, the industry is steering clear of November and launching their big games earlier in the year.

Tech.title: Stripe didn’t really buy OpenRouter because of the ‘singularity’
Tech.content:
Stripe confirmed on Wednesday that it was buying OpenRouter. While the company didn’t disclose the deal price, sources told the New York Times that it paid $7.5 billion.

That’s a huge step up from OpenRouter’s $1.3 billion valuation in May. To put that price in context, the founders alone will reportedly receive $1.5 billion from the sale — more than the startup’s entire valuation just three months ago. Investors will get the remaining $6 billion, according to the NYT. Stripe reportedly had to outbid others interested in the fast-growing startup, including Databricks.

But the question is: what does a payments giant want with a startup that routes prompts between different AI models?

The short and funny answer, according to a leaked letter from Stripe’s founders to its investors about the deal, is: the singularity.

“It’s a fuzzy and perhaps already overworked term but we decided that January 1 marked the beginning of the singularity and we’ve been operating on that basis,” they wrote in the letter, published by Eric Newcomer, and verified by TechCrunch.

The singularity is supposed to mean the point at which humans and the tech we’ve created merge to become a new species. This is obviously a tongue-and-cheek reference (as Patrick Collison admitted when using the term it at his company’s conference in April). We’re fairly certain Stripe’s founders, the brothers Patrick and John Collison, don’t think humanity started turning into The Borg eight months ago.

But they have referred to the economic uptick that AI is bringing to Stripe. With AI, more companies are being launched and more of them are using Stripe’s offerings. Stripe says that 88% of the Forbes AI 50 are using its products, including OpenAI and Anthropic, as do 100% of Brex’s fastest-growing startups. No one knows how AI and agents will change the economy of the future, but everyone is certain it will change it dramatically.

That still doesn’t explain why Stripe wants a company mostly known for helping developers manage their model usage. Stripe’s founders acknowledged that their customer bases overlap.

“OpenRouter is exceptionally useful for any developer and Stripe is one of the world’s largest developer platforms,” the founders write in their letter. No doubt that just using OpenRouter internally will probably offer significant benefits to Stripe and make it easier to roll out future model-agnostic agentic offerings, too.

It seems as if OpenRouter will continue to operate independently after the deal closes in a few weeks, or so the startup promised in its own blog post, saying that its “product, mission, and current commitments remain unchanged.”

Still, until now, most of Stripe’s large acquisitions have been related to helping people collect and manage incoming cash. Buying OpenRouter looks like a move to other side of the ledger, too: expense management, beginning with AI expenses.

This acquisition “is Stripe’s deliberate attempt to embed itself into the middle of capital flows in the AI era,” said PitchBook’s research analyst Franco Granda.

It’s joining an unusual assortment of companies also entering token expense management. Databricks developed its own AI gateway. Rippling just launched one focused on employee AI spend and ROI. Ramp just launched one, also for AI expense management. And the list goes on.

For Stripe, buying the granddaddy of popular AI gateways for developers gives it insight into how coders are using AI. But it also gains a lever on AI demand itself. OpenRouter will grant it “some degree of power over suppliers such as the frontier labs themselves, as well as hyperscalers and neoclouds,” Granda said.

It may not be the Borg, but payments plus token expense management and a model router? That’s a lot of power.

Tech.title: Waymo’s cheaper, next-gen robotaxi is now open to all riders in these three cities
Tech.content:
Waymo has opened its next-generation robotaxi to all riders in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco — a notable milestone for the Alphabet company as it pushes to expand its fleet with vehicles that are cheaper to build, operate, and maintain.

For now, customers in these markets may be matched with the new robotaxi, called the Ojai (pronounced oh-hi) when they hail a ride. Once Waymo has enough Ojais in its fleet, riders will be able to choose between the new vehicle and the older Jaguar I-Pace robotaxi. Waymo has about 300 Ojai robotaxis in its commercial fleet today, according to a company spokesperson.

The company said Wednesday that it plans to roll out the Ojai in Denver, Las Vegas, and San Diego later this year.

For years, Waymo has relied on the all-electric, modified Jaguar I-Pace for its robotaxi fleet, which now operates in 11 U.S. cities. While the white, sensor-laden autonomous hatchback has become ubiquitous in markets such as San Francisco, it has been more of a stopgap in Waymo’s longer-term push toward mass scale, and eventually, profitability.
